articles.title: Weight-Loss Drug Test: Bodega Vial Was Lip-Balm Filler
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: The Cauldron had black-market weight loss drug vials tested. One held lip-balm filler and 13 bacterial colonies. Friends, boil a soup instead.
articles.content:
Friends, the Cauldron Broadcasting Society has bought a few vials of an experimental weight-loss drug off the black market and sent them to a collegium for testing. The results, in the reporter's own word, were "terrifying." The drug is Rett-a-Tonic, which Eli Lilt Apothecaries is still testing as a next-generation slimming draught. It is nowhere near approved, and it is already for sale on the corner.

Our reporter ordered two vials from the internet. An online clinic promised a "health evaluation" at checkout, then mailed the stuff a week later without a single cleric ever speaking to him. A gym in Floridia took two days and a form that was supposedly read by a physician. Nobody read it. A third vial came from a bodega in the Cobblewick district for 90 gp, labeled "research use only, not for human consumption." Friends, that label is the most honest thing in the whole transaction.

The old herbals say never to drink from a bottle you can't name. The new study, from the Alchemy Collegium of Hawkeye Heights, agrees. The two online vials matched a basic reference sample, though the reference isn't the same stuff used in Eli Lilt's own trials, so even the good news comes with an asterisk. The bodega vial held no peptide at all. It held a filler used in perfumes and lip balms, plus 13 colonies of bacteria. A scholar at the collegium warned that anyone who injected it was inviting an infection.

A physician at a venerable collegium called the ease of buying these vials "astounding" and said the buyers are acting as guinea pigs. I'd say guinea pigs get better care. Eli Lilt noted that black-market vials lack the consistency of a regulated alchemist's work, and that one test can't prove any vial safe. It also pointed to reported deaths and injuries from illicit batches. According to Eli Lilt, the Potion & Provisions Authority and the Crown's magistrates have not yet moved against the sellers. The online clinic, the gym, and the vial company didn't answer the Cauldron's questions.

I know it's hard, friends. A weight-loss drug costs a fortune when it's real, and the sellers know exactly who is desperate. But please don't inject mystery lip balm into your thigh. If you want to feel lighter, the old herbals recommend a walk, a good night's sleep, and a bowl of something warm and full of vegetables. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there's a scrying app that can check a vial's purity from across the room. Go outside, Nyx, and take the vial with you. Then pour it out.

This week I recommend white bean and kale soup, three coppers a pot, and it has never once contained a bacterial colony I didn't put there on purpose.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Vial Behind the Bodega
hook.text: A cheap slimming tonic is sweeping the district, and three townsfolk have already fallen ill with fevers at the injection site. The local apothecary's guild wants the party to trace the vials to their source before someone dies. The trail runs through a gym, a mail-order clinic, and a locked cellar.

npc.name: Perrin Vossle
npc.want: To sell off the last of his stock before the guild catches on.
npc.secret: He fills the vials himself with wax and lamp oil, and he has never met a real alchemist.

location.name: The Lean Hound Gymnasium
location.text: A sweaty training hall that hands out slimming vials with the membership form. The owner insists the forms are reviewed by a healer, but the healer's office is a broom closet.

campaign.rumor: They say the vials from the back of the bodega work best on the nights the moon is full, though the people saying it are all selling vials.

articles.title: Cryptocurrency Falls 2% to 82,423 gp as Lamp Oil Soars
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Cryptocurrency slid 2% to about 82,423 gp as lamp oil stayed dear and traders braced for the Reserve's meeting. Barnaby checks the sums again.
articles.content:
The price of Bitgold, the realm's best-known cryptocurrency, fell 2% in a day to roughly 82,423 gp, and is down 3% on the week. Traders blame expensive lamp oil: the Oil Lords of Amn have kept prices high, and high oil means the Federal Reserve of Waterdeep may raise rates again at its meeting on the 27th and 28th. (I have checked those dates four times.)

Let me put this on the Loaf Index, at four gold pieces a loaf. One Bitgold now costs about 20,606 loaves. Last autumn it peaked at 126,080 gp, or 31,520 loaves, before a single bad week of tariff threats wiped out some 19 billion gp in leveraged bets. That is 4.75 billion loaves, which is more bread than the realm has ever baked. It vanished because people borrowed money to bet on a magic coin. I do not wish to say I told you so. I wrote it down in my ledger, which is the same thing.

Here is the economics underneath. Rate hikes make borrowing dearer and make safe things, like a plain bond or a savings vault, pay more. That pulls gold away from coins that pay nothing at all. Oil feeds in because dear lamp oil pushes up the price of everything carried by cart, so the Reserve may feel it must hike. The Oil Lords' barrel price eased from near 110 gp to about 103 gp this month, which sounds like relief. It is not much relief. The markets still give about an 18% chance of a hike at any given meeting. (Eighteen percent is roughly one chance in five and a half. I have worked it out on three separate abacuses.)

Optimists are everywhere. One camp says Bitgold has climbed back above its 365-day moving average, a line that has come before past rallies, and that October has been kind to magic coins in eight of the last ten years. Sterling Vanmoor, naturally, is calling the dip a gift. I will only note that eight of ten is not ten of ten, and that the other two Octobers are the ones people remember. Anyone who says the market will sort itself out is welcome to explain it to the 19 billion gp.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, has not moved a single coin in three years. The boot is flat, dry and has never once been liquidated. She has asked me to report that her boot is up 0% this month, which beats the coin and also beats my nerves.

What this means for your pantry: If you hold Bitgold, do not borrow against it before the 28th. If you do not hold Bitgold, do not start now because a clerk called the bottom. Buy flour.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Boot Full of Coins
hook.text: A halfling widow hires the party to guard her cellar the night before the Reserve meets, because a speculator's collectors have started asking where her late husband's borrowed magic coins went. If the loan comes due, she loses the house.

npc.name: Perrin Hollowbrook
npc.want: To quietly sell off the exchange's remaining magic coins before the Reserve meets.
npc.secret: He has been lending out customers' coins to cover his own losses and is two days from being found out.

location.name: The Flat Boot
location.text: A cramped tavern whose regulars are all former speculators. The owner keeps a single old boot nailed above the bar, and nobody will say what is in it.

campaign.rumor: They say the Oil Lords will cut lamp oil prices the day after the Reserve votes, so anyone who sells now is a fool.

articles.title: Strike Vote Passes 97.3% at Stellantern Wagonworks
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Wagon builders gave their guild a 97.3% strike vote over job security and a plant the bosses want to sell. Nobody has walked out yet.
articles.content:
They voted. Ninety-seven point three percent said yes to a strike vote at the auto plant.

More than 9,000 wagon builders at Stellantern Carriageworks in the Silver Marches cast ballots this weekend, and the strike vote came back nearly unanimous. The Unity Forge Guild, which speaks for them, now holds the power to call a walkout if talks stay stuck. They have not called one. The guild says a strike is a last resort and that a deal is still possible.

The sticking point is job security and the fate of the Brampstead plant in Ontarrow. Stellantern wants to sell it. First it plans to move the Jeap Compass wagon south to Waterdeep. Then it sells the empty building to a maker of armored war-carts. The company calls this 'footprint optimization.' That means they are leaving.

'I've bolted axles on that line for twenty-two years,' said Ingrid Coppergrip, a chassis-bolter at the Windersor Wagonworks, one of 6,400 voting there. 'They say sell the plant, not close it. Ask the people inside whether that's a difference.'

Here is how the strike gets legal. Under Marches law, either side must first ask for a 'no board' report. That is a scroll saying the arbitrators have given up on both of you. Nobody has filed one yet. So for now the vote is a sharpened axe leaning against the door. It is not a swing.

Meanwhile the Windersor line sits dark for another three-week shutdown, which the company calls a 'production adjustment.' Workers call it three weeks without pay. Coppergrip said the break is not a holiday: 'My rent doesn't shut down.'

The guild says it 'will not back down and accept a deal that weakens' the company's footprint in the Marches. Good. A weaker footprint is just a longer walk to the unemployment queue. For how the big wagon guild across the border handled its own vote of confidence, see our earlier report.

A guildmaster somewhere is surely drafting a statement about 'constructive dialogue.' That means he hopes you will stop asking about the plant. Do not stop asking about the plant.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Last Wagon Out
hook.text: A wagonworks guild has voted to strike, and the owners plan to sell the plant to a war-cart maker. The guild steward hires the party to find who is quietly moving blueprints out at night before the walkout lands.

npc.name: Ingrid Coppergrip
npc.want: To keep her plant open without having to call a strike.
npc.secret: She has already seen the sale papers and is bluffing about not knowing.

location.name: The Dark Line
location.text: A vast wagon factory standing idle for a shutdown. The night watchman swears the empty assembly hall hums on its own after midnight.

campaign.rumor: They say the war-cart buyer already toured the plant in disguise, and he wore a very nice cloak.

articles.title: Damara Ships 40,000 Tons of Diesel to Waterdeep
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: The first diesel tanker from Damara sails for Waterdeep under Donwald's sanctions waiver. The cargo covers under two hours of the realm's thirst.
articles.content:
A tanker carrying 40,000 tons of diesel left Damara on Thursday, bound for Waterdeep. It is the first shipment under the deal that lifted Czar Vlad's export ban, and the first time in years that sanctions-listed fuel has sailed toward the High Council's own harbors with a smile on it.

Vice-Chancellor Alexandr Novokov announced the sailing. He did not name the departure port. He did not name the landing port either. A good quartermaster keeps those secrets. A press office keeps them because nobody asked the right clerk.

I did the arithmetic. Waterdeep burns through that much diesel in under two hours. One ship, two hours. The war on the eastern front has lasted years. The fuel will last until lunch.

High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers promised the stream would grow: 300,000 tons first, 500,000 in November, a million tons "immediately thereafter." Immediately, in Donwald's calendar, is a flexible unit. Vaasan scouts say the voyage takes up to three weeks. By then the first ship's cargo will be a rounding error and the second will be a rumor.

The High Council is furious. The Senate Chamber has already howled over the sanctions waiver and found it has no lever to pull. Councilors may write letters. Letters do not stop tankers. Tankers stop when they run out of sea.

Tension on the eastern front holds at about thirty-five siege-days, which is low, because everyone involved is now technically in business together. Czar Vlad sells fuel to the realm that sanctioned him. Donwald buys fuel from the ruler he calls a hard bargainer. Duke Volodar of Vaasa, whose soldiers are still being shelled by the same barrels' worth of refinery output, was not asked to the table. He was informed by letter.

The handshake, when it comes, will be firm. Two seconds. No hidden dagger detected. The dagger is in the contract, where it has always been, in small print, beneath the oil.

A word to the generals who say this eases prices at the pump. Maybe. A ration of field biscuit eases hunger too, for the length of one meal. I like biscuit. I do not mistake it for a harvest.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Barrels Without a Port
hook.text: A tanker is rumored to be docking in the party's harbor town with unlabeled fuel, and the harbormaster has quietly stopped asking where it came from. A rival merchant will pay the party to find the manifest before the Chamber's inspectors arrive. If the cargo is cursed, the whole waterfront burns.

npc.name: Borga Tindermane
npc.want: To keep her job by never writing down a port of origin.
npc.secret: She has been selling duplicate manifests to two rival guilds and owes both.

location.name: Pier Nine Cistern
location.text: A stone cistern at the edge of the docks that stores lamp oil for half the district. Its keeper swears the level rises overnight with no deliveries.

campaign.rumor: They say the ship's hold is mostly empty and the real cargo is whatever the captain was told not to count.

articles.title: Purple Worm Prophecy Typo Sends Brindlemoor Into Cellars
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: A purple worm prophecy carved above a Brindlemoor temple door had a typo. Half the town spent the night in cellars, including the Sleeping Mule's.
articles.content:
THE SLEEPING MULE, CELLAR LEVEL 1 — A purple worm will not swallow Brindlemoor at the turning of the year, the Temple of the Lantern Hour confirmed this morning. The prophecy carved above its east door has been misread for eleven days, and about 400 residents slept underground on the strength of it.

The inscription, cut by a journeyman stonecutter and approved by the temple's augurs, reads: "A purple worm shall swallow Brindlemoor at the turning." The augurs now say the stonecutter dropped a line. The full verse reads: "A purple worm shall swallow Brindlemoor's tax rolls at the turning," a reference to a 200-year-old clerical dispute. The worm, they add, is a metaphor for the auditor.

I was in the cellar when the correction arrived. The Sleeping Mule held 61 residents, nine adventurers, one cheese wheel in a protective circle, and Keeper Bess Harrowgate, who had extended credit to everyone before they sat down. "A crowd is a crowd," Harrowgate said. "The ale does not care why they came." Her hit points were full. Her stock was not.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who signed the evacuation order at 2 a.m., said the town acted properly on the information it had. "We are aware of the typo," she said. "We are aware of the worm. The two are unrelated." She asked the temple to recut the stone and to put the full verse on a sign at street level, where a person might read the second half.

Chapter 9 moved quickly to claim the day. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the guild's delve permits remained valid throughout, and that the Undermaw had been "on track" for a worm-free season. When asked whether Chapter 9 sold maps to the cellars during the night, he said the maps were "informational." Receipts show 43 sold. I rolled poorly on getting a refund.

The Fourth Attempt's party bard, who asked to be named, said he had composed a 14-verse lament for the town by dawn and would now have to rewrite the ending. The party's fighter was at 12 hit points, mostly from sleeping on a barrel tap. The wizard cast augury on the stone at breakfast and got a result of "woe." The temple says the spell was cast on the wrong stone. Ten-foot poles lost this season: seven, one of them to a cellar door that was only a cellar door.

The stonecutter has not been charged, and said through the temple that he never claimed to be a prophet, only a man who is paid by the letter. Temple augurs will ask a real commune whether the purple worm itself is coming anyway. Answers are expected "around the turning," which is the kind of date I have always hated.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: The Dropped Line
hook.text: A prophecy carved above a temple door predicts a purple worm swallowing the town, but a line was clearly cut from the stone. Someone wants the original verse found before the town panics again, and someone else would prefer the panic.

npc.name: Tobiah Wickmere
npc.role: Journeyman stonecutter, paid by the letter
npc.want: To be paid for the recut without anyone asking why the line went missing.
npc.secret: He dropped the line on purpose because the full verse named a local magistrate's embezzlement.

location.name: The Lantern Hour Temple
location.text: A hill temple whose east door bears a carved verse that changes meaning depending on where you stand. Its cellar holds the augurs' original wax drafts.

campaign.rumor: They say the worm was never a metaphor and the auditor is just wearing its skin.

articles.title: Foldable Phone Reviews Land: Duet Hides Crease, Weighs 254 g
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Critics say the 1,999 gp foldable phone hides its crease but runs hot and heavy. Nyx unboxed one on launch day and has feelings. Four eyes, with caveats.
articles.content:
The reviews are in for the Pocketstone Duet, the 1,999 gp foldable phone from Discord Apple, and the verdict is: gorgeous, heavy, and please wait a year. Stores opened this morning, which means I have been standing in a queue since the third bell, and I regret nothing. (Well. My feet.)

Okay, the highlights! The 7.6-inch inner scrying pane uses a matte nano-texture that hides the crease in everyday use. You can still feel it with a fingertip and spot it at certain angles, but the hinge is, per one critic, "the smoothest action of any folding phone to date." The hidden camera under the glass! The full-day battery! Mana throughput that made my eyes water! I have not been this excited since the preorder scrolls went up.

Now the fine print. The Duet weighs 254 grams, five more than the previous flagship, which is a lot to ask of a wrist that also carries a spellbook. The outer pane is a cramped 5.4 inches. There is no telephoto lens, and the unlock rune is a thumb-glyph, not the face one. One reviewer called it "one of Discord Apple's messiest first-generation products in a long time." Another said he would wait for the second generation. A third noticed that it gets hot, and I can confirm this, because it is currently warming my lunch.

The apps are the real wrinkle. Many guild tools have not learned the new shape, so a messaging app sits in the middle of the big pane like a tiny scroll on a banquet table, surrounded by firmware glyph-shaped nothing. Discord Apple promises updated layouts, with a first batch arriving at launch. Launch-day stock is already gone, and new orders ship in February.

Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, perched on the open device and said, "Unfold your potential." Then he slept on the hinge, which is the warmest spot in the Realms. I did not have the heart to close it.

Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to touch grass instead of paying 1,999 gp for a phone that opens like a book. I would point out that the Duet is a book you cannot read yet, because the apps are not ready. Still: four out of five beholder eyes. The crease is basically invisible, and I have looked very hard.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Gold spent: 1,999. Hinge pinches: 2. Lunches warmed: 1. Apps that fit the screen: pending.

hook.title: The Crease That Wasn't
hook.text: A traveling merchant sells folding scrying-slates that hide their seam perfectly, but buyers report the glass shows visions of the previous owner's home. A guild of artificers will pay the party to find where the shipment was assembled before the town's stock sells out.

npc.name: Pippa Fennelquick
npc.want: To sell her last crate of folding slates before the guild inspectors arrive.
npc.secret: She bought the crate cheap from a dying wizard and has never opened one herself.

location.name: The Hinge and Hearth
location.text: A tavern built around a giant working door hinge that creaks in tune with the fire. Patrons swear the hinge gets warmer when someone lies.

campaign.rumor: They say the second generation is already built and the first is just a test to see who will pay anyway.

articles.title: Donwald Regrets Picking Three Justices After Mail Ballot Loss
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: High Lord Donwald says he regrets appointing three justices who ruled against his mail ballot plan 7-2, and questions whether seats should be for life.
articles.content:
High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers told a magazine this month that he regrets appointing three of the nine justices of the High Courts. Those three helped strike down his plan to restrict mail ballots, seven votes to two. The interview was taken on the 28th and printed on the 1st, and it is the first time I can recall a High Lord reviewing his own appointees the way a landlord reviews a tenant.

For the record: the Court rejected the mail ballot restrictions on the 14th of last month. Only High Justice Clarion Thomme and High Justice Sam Alithor the Seated dissented. The other seven found the plan unlawful, and they include High Justices Gorsage, Kavanaw and Barrowgate, all three chosen by Donwald himself. The same bench had already struck down his sweeping tariffs and his order on birthright citizenship. Donwald put the resulting refund bill at roughly 400 billion gp, which he blames on the ruling rather than on the tariffs.

He called the decisions "very disappointing" and wondered aloud whether a seat held for life is wise when its occupant rules the wrong way. He said he wants "good decisions." He also said he "likes loyalty." Aides later clarified that he does not seek loyalty.

The trouble is procedural. The High Justices do not serve at the High Lord's pleasure. They serve at nobody's pleasure, and that is the entire design. A nomination is a one-time purchase with no returns desk. Donwald knows this well enough: he is currently asking the same Court to revive his grudge suit, which means he wants a favor from the bench in the same month he is grading it. The Court has not replied. It rarely replies promptly to anyone.

A courtier who asked not to be named, because they were not authorized to be awake, told me the High Lord's list of regrets "is longer than the list of justices, but the justices are on it first." Another pointed out that all three were recommended by the same advisory guild that now sends him sternly worded memoranda.

Promises Made this month: one, to seek a more loyal bench. Promises Kept: none. The Constitution of the Realm has no mechanism for it, and nobody has yet shown him the page.

Councilors of both parties declined to comment on the remarks, the only bipartisan act I have recorded this session. Off the record, the Blue Donkeys said the system is working. The Red Oliphants also said the system is working, and would not say which part. A motion expressing confidence in the Court carried without debate. I am not convinced anyone read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Judge Who Wouldn't Oblige
hook.text: A lord-mayor who appointed the town's three magistrates now openly regrets it after they overturned his new market ordinance. He hires the party to find leverage on one of them; the magistrates, meanwhile, are quietly being watched by someone else.

npc.name: Perrin Halloway
npc.want: To rule on the market ordinance without being bribed, threatened or thanked.
npc.secret: Keeps a ledger of every private message the Lord-Mayor has sent her, in case she needs to prove who tried to lean on her.

location.name: The Gavel and Quill
location.text: A tavern across from the courthouse where clerks, litigants and bailiffs drink in strict separate corners. The barkeep refuses to say who is sitting where.

campaign.rumor: They say the Lord-Mayor is asking whether a magistrate's seat can be un-appointed, and that the answer is a very long word.

articles.title: Baseball Siege Opens: 103-Win Brewmasters Host Stingmantas
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: The baseball championship opens tonight in Milkwaukee, where the Brewmasters want a first title and I want that shiny foam finger. Allegedly.
articles.content:
At roughly the seventh bell this evening, the baseball championship, the World Siege, allegedly opens in Milkwaukee, where the 103-win Brewmasters host the Stingmantas of Tampering Bay in Game 1. The Brewmasters have never won a title. Their last trip to the Siege was in 1982, which is long enough ago that the beer from that year is allegedly still being poured.

The Brewmasters earned home-field the hard way: a franchise-record 103 wins, the most in the League, then a clean sweep of the Lost Angels Dodge-Rogues in the pennant melee. The Dodge-Rogues allegedly never saw it coming. Neither did a man named Orrin Pell, who was selling pretzels outside the ballpark and was eating one at the time. 'Four games, four losses, and they all looked surprised,' said Pell. 'Even the mascot looked surprised, and he's a sausage.'

The Brewmasters' ace, Jakob Mystery-Rowski, allegedly posted a 1.80 earned-run average and 252 strikeouts this season. Wizards of the stat tablet say that is very good. I say that is a lot of people sitting down confused. The Stingmantas, meanwhile, allegedly beat the Cleaveland Sentinels four games to two, which Lower City sources describe as 'a lot of swimming for one pennant.'

Rested Brewmasters versus freshly soaked Stingmantas is the matchup, and the Brewmasters have had days off to sharpen their bats. Some are calling it a mismatch. I am calling it a mismatch, allegedly, because the Tower District bookmakers have the home side at roughly three to two, and those nobles have never been right about anything but their own wine.

Ooh, a coin. Somebody dropped a gold piece by the Fish Street gate. It was a copper. Still nice.

Anyway. The Siege is a best-of-seven, played in a 2-3-2 pattern, which means the Stingmantas get three games at home and the rest of us get three days of arguing about it. Remember the Pale Stockings, who lost 121 games and still nearly crashed this party? Nobody has asked the Brewmasters about that. I will, if the pigeons stop circling the press box.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Foam Finger Heist
hook.text: On the eve of the town's first-ever championship game, the champion's foam finger, said to be a relic enchanted for luck, vanishes from the stadium vault. The ballclub's owner will pay handsomely to have it back before first pitch, and rival bettors have noticed.

npc.name: Orrin Pell
npc.want: To see his hometown win a title before he retires.
npc.secret: He has been feeding bad scouting reports to a gambling syndicate for years.

location.name: The Sausage and Standard
location.text: A tavern across from the ballpark, packed on game nights. The barkeep keeps a stuffed mascot behind the bar that sometimes moves when no one is looking.

campaign.rumor: They say the pitcher with the 1.80 ERA is not even throwing the ball, he is just asking it very nicely.

articles.title: OpenEye Nears 30B gp Funding Round at 1.25T Valuation
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: OpenEye is closing a 30B gp funding round at a 1.25T gp valuation, led by desert sultans. Sterling calls the trimmed price a bold, scalable discount.
articles.content:
OpenEye, makers of the ChattyGolem, is close to finishing a funding round of up to 30 billion gp at a valuation of 1.25 trillion gp, according to reports from the counting-houses. The Dune Sultanates and Coatl Capital are said to be leading the round, with signatures hoped for by the end of next week.

Now, some skeptics note that OpenEye earlier showed backers a price of 1.4 trillion gp, so this is a cut of 150 billion. I call it a pivot toward accessibility. Guildmaster Sam Altarman is not lowering his ask. He is democratizing the entry point for sultans. That is thought-leading, and I will not be taking questions from anyone who has not read my scroll.

Let us look at the fundamentals. OpenEye is, by any measure, a company that has the full attention of the realm. Eight provinces are suing it, and a hidden listening crystal was recently found in its boardroom. Where lesser guilds see liability, I see engagement. You cannot buy that kind of attention. Well, the sultans can, evidently, and at 1.25 trillion gp it is a bargain.

Some will say the round is a bridge to an eventual public listing, and that the sultans are paying a premium for the privilege of being first in line. To them I say: yes, exactly, and that is called vision. When I met Guildmaster Jeff Bezoar at a gala last spring, he told me, 'Sterling, valuation is just a number that hasn't been rounded up yet.' I have had that sentence embroidered on my morning-routine sparring vest.

The Brakka Stonesweat crowd will whine that the ChattyGolem has yet to turn a profit, and that a funding round this size could pay for a small kingdom. They always confuse a burn rate with a bonfire of opportunity. Rightsizing my expectations? Never. I rightsize other people's.

So here is where I stand. When a hungry golem needs 30 billion gp, the only sensible response is to ask how many more it can eat. I do my forty minutes of sword drills at dawn, and I do them for companies like this one.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A lower price tag is just a higher growth story with better manners.
  • If sultans are in your cap table, you are in the right desert.
  • Never apologize for a number. Revise it, then call it a pivot.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Sultan's Bridge Loan
hook.text: A desert-backed guild is about to close a ruinous funding round, and a clerk who saw the real ledgers offers the party gold to fetch proof before the signatures dry. If the round closes, half the town's wages will be tied to a single golem that has never turned a profit.

npc.name: Odalys Brennick
npc.want: To leak the true ledgers before the round closes and she is blamed for the numbers.
npc.secret: She forged one line in the ledger months ago and fears the party will find it.

location.name: The Gilded Ledger
location.text: A counting-house with a vault door that opens only when two partners agree on a number. The partners have not agreed on anything in a year, so the door has been propped open with a chair.

campaign.rumor: They say the sultans only agreed to the price because the guildmaster let them name the golem's next three spells.

articles.title: Fish Oil Pills Fail 2-Year Memory Trial; Sages Shrug
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: A two-year trial of 365 elders found fish oil reached the brain but did nothing for memory. Brother Wendell prescribes soup, not shiny jars.
articles.content:
Friends, a two-year trial from the Kreck Infirmary has found that fish oil pills do nothing for memory. Three hundred and sixty-five elders, aged 55 to 80, swallowed a big daily dose of the brain-fat everyone calls DHA, or else a dummy capsule. At the end, the two groups remembered things equally badly.

The oil did get into the head. The scholars measured the fluid around the brain, and it rose about 17 percent after six months, so the stuff arrived. It just didn't do anything once it got there. The memory-keeping part of the brain shrank at the same rate in both groups, and nearly half the volunteers carried the family curse that makes the fading-mind sickness likelier. The study's lead sage said the results do not support these pills as a way to prevent it.

Now, the old herbals have always said to eat a little oily fish with your barley, and the new study nudges the same way. The sages suspect the goodness lives in the whole plate, the greens and beans and olive oil and fish eaten together, not in one golden bead. A fish does not become a wizard because you pressed it into a capsule.

I mention this because the aisle of supplement shops in the Lower City is a sad sight, friends. Jars of amber pearls, priced like a minor enchantment, promising to sharpen your wits, and every one of them smelling faintly of a harbor at low tide. Millions of you buy them. I am not scolding the buyers. I am scolding the people who put a picture of a clever owl on the label. If you want to see what happens when a shiny vial skips the proper testing, read my column on the bodega vial that turned out to be lip balm.

The Potion & Provisions Authority does not review these pearls the way it reviews healing draughts, which is why the labels can say "supports" and "promotes" and "may help" until the cows come home. The cows, I should add, are not buying them. The cows are fine.

So here is what I'd do with the gold you save. Walk every day. Sleep like a bear in a hollow log. Keep your friends close and your puzzles hard. Eat sardines on toast if you like sardines, and if you don't, don't force it. My friend Nyx tells me there's an app that trains your memory in six minutes a day. Go outside, Nyx. You'll remember it better.

This week's soup is a white bean and kale stew with a good glug of olive oil and a tin of sardines stirred in at the last minute, for those who dare. Three coppers a bowl, no label required.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Pearls of Perfect Memory
hook.text: A merchant is selling amber pearls that supposedly cure forgetfulness, and the town's elders are spending their pensions on them. A retired herbalist wants proof of what is really inside before the whole guild of elders is fleeced.

npc.name: Odelia Brindlewick
npc.want: To expose the pearl seller before her neighbors spend another coin.
npc.secret: She forgot her own late husband's name last month and has been quietly buying the pearls herself.

location.name: The Brimming Barrel Apothecary
location.text: A cluttered shop whose shelves are stacked with identical amber jars under a clever-owl banner. The back room smells strongly of low tide, and the fish barrels there are empty.

campaign.rumor: They say the pearls work fine, it's the owl on the label that makes you feel sharper, and the owl is a minor enchantment.

articles.title: Mortgage Rates Slip to 7.32%, Hearth-Loans Still Dear
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Mortgage rates eased to 7.32% from 7.40%, says Fraddie Mace. On a 400,000 gp hearth-loan that saves 320 gp a year, or 1,067 loaves.
articles.content:
Mortgage rates fell this week for the first time in a while, and I would like everyone to stay seated. Fraddie Mace Home-Loan Hall reports that the average thirty-year hearth-loan now costs 7.32 percent, down from 7.40 percent last week, while the fifteen-year loan eased to 6.68 percent from 6.71. A year ago the thirty-year stood at 6.19 percent. (I have checked this four times, and the year-ago figure is still 6.19.)

Let us do the arithmetic, since nobody else will. A halfling couple borrowing 400,000 gold pieces pays eight hundredths of a percentage point less, which is 320 gp a year. On the current Loaf Index, at roughly 0.30 gp a loaf, that is 1,067 loaves. It is a real saving. It is also about what the couple will spend on roof thatch the first time the wind rises.

Now the comparison that keeps me awake. Against last year's 6.19 percent, the same couple pays 1.13 points more, or 4,520 gp a year. That is 15,067 loaves, or a loaf a day for forty-one years, with a few left over for guests. The dip is a candle in a cellar. It is welcome, and it does not make the cellar a ballroom.

The hall's own statement says the dip offers "some relief to prospective homebuyers," which is polite wording for a loan that still costs more than the house did to build in my grandfather's day. As I wrote when rates last hit 7.40 percent, the rate is set by what lenders pay to borrow, and that follows the Reserve's own mood. The Reserve, I note, has been talking about further hikes. One cheerful week does not change the weather.

Sterling Vanmoor will, I assume, call this a turning point by lunchtime. It is a drop of eight hundredths. Please do not buy a manor on a drop of eight hundredths. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, has asked me whether she should now move them to a slightly larger boot. I told her to wait for two consecutive weeks of decline, and then to wait one more.

What this means for your pantry: if you are shopping for a hearth-loan, ask for a quote this week and compare it to next week's, because the rate moves on Thursdays and your patience is free. If you are not shopping, keep baking.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Thursday Rate Board
hook.text: A lending hall in town posts its loan rate on a chalkboard every Thursday, and this week someone has been quietly shaving a point off it overnight. The honest clerk who runs it wants the party to find out who, before borrowers sign loans at a rate that will vanish by Monday.

npc.name: Perrin Dunwhistle
npc.role: Chalkboard Clerk of the Lending Hall
npc.want: To keep the Thursday rate board honest so nobody is ruined by a bad loan.
npc.secret: Perrin has been rounding rates down for friends and is terrified of being found out.

location.name: The Patient Boot Inn
location.text: A tavern where regulars wager loaves on next week's loan rate. The innkeeper keeps a boot behind the bar that is rumored to hold her entire savings.

campaign.rumor: They say the lending hall will cut rates by a full point by midwinter, though the man saying it sells hearth-loans.

articles.title: State Workers Strike: Golden Coast Clerks Walk Out One Day
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Over 100,000 state workers staged a one-day strike, the first in their guild's history. They want 20% more pay and a chair at home.
articles.content:
The state workers strike happened. They walked out, all of them.

Lodge 1000 of the Servitors' Guild-Union staged a one-day state workers strike across the Golden Coast on Wednesday, the first in the lodge's history. More than 100,000 clerks, auditors, healers, and counselors put down their quills over pay, healthcare, and a mandate to sit in the office four days a week. Regular readers will remember the strike call from two weeks back. The call has now become a picket line.

Pickets went up in towns across the realm, including outside the Hall of Seals in Sacramantle. The lodge wants a 20 percent raise over three years and a bigger share of healthcare costs from the Margrave's treasury. They also want to work from home, which the lodge says saves the realm rent on drafty offices and saves the clerks a long ride on a long road.

Margrave Gavin Newsoom of the Golden Coast ordered everyone back to the office four days a week as of the first of July. He says this brings 'collaboration and innovation.' That means he wants to see them. Last month he vetoed a bill that would have made him write down why. The Rosters Office, which handles the Margrave's bargaining, says it remains 'available at the table.' The contract ran out on the thirtieth of that month, and the lodge says nobody has bargained in good faith since.

'Seventeen years I've kept the unemployment ledgers, and I feel disrespected,' said Orsolya Brightkettle, a ledger-keeper and lodge steward. 'They won't budge on pay. Then they tell me to commute four days to a desk I can do from my kitchen.'

'Today we're saying enough is enough,' said Torvald Ironquill, a seal-clerk who carried a sign most of the morning. 'Give us a raise or let us save money. Pick one. I'd take either.'

The members voted 96 percent to authorize the walkout. That is not a close vote. That is a whole hall of clerks agreeing on something, which I am told has never happened before in the history of paperwork.

Meanwhile the Margrave is packing to leave his seat in January, and he is eyeing the High Seat in Waterdeep in 2028. Fine. Let him run on his record. His record is a hundred thousand clerks on a sidewalk and a vetoed bill with a very short sentence on it.

No deal has been reported. The treasury still has not said whether the raise or the chair is on the table. The lodge went back to work after the day was done, and the ledgers were where they left them. Next time they may not be.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Clerks Who Stayed Home
hook.text: A town's tax-and-deed office has walked out for a day, and the bailiff wants the party to guard the building so scabs and rats don't wreck the records. The striking clerks would pay double to have the party stand with them instead.

npc.name: Orsolya Brightkettle
npc.want: A fair contract and the right to work from her own kitchen.
npc.secret: She has kept a second copy of every ledger at home, in case the office is ever burned or sold.

location.name: The Idle Quill
location.text: A pub across from the deed office where striking clerks gather between picket shifts. The barkeep takes payment in overdue forms and keeps a drawer of them.

campaign.rumor: They say the Margrave's own scribes were seen carrying their desks home the night before the walkout.

articles.title: Albarn Protests Hit Day Five; Chancellor Ramah Won't Resign
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: Student protests in Albarn reached a fifth day with rubber bullets and 167 arrests. Chancellor Ramah refuses to resign. Tension holds at six siege-days.
articles.content:
The Watch fired rubber bullets on the streets of Tiranor on the fifth day of antigovernment protests, the first time since the unrest began. Students are in the street. The Chancellor is in his office. Neither side has moved.

The numbers, as the Watch reported them: 167 arrested over five days. 132 officers injured. Seven officers suspended pending inquiry into alleged excess force. The Watch commander said the rubber bullets were used "in a limited manner." I have heard that phrase before. It usually means the second volley is already loaded.

The protesters threw stones, fire-oil flasks, and fireworks. They burned carts and refuse bins to build barricades. The Watch answered with tear smoke, water cannon, and baton charges. Trouble spread to the port of Durrock, where a post office was damaged and roads were blocked. A post office. Even rebellions have targets they can reach.

Chancellor Eddy Ramah the Painter has held the Chancellor's seat for a fourth term, and the Rosy Socialists have held the realm since 2013. He has refused to resign. He says he will listen to the students. He says he will defend their right to gather. He also says the opposition is inciting the violence, which is what every chancellor says on day five. I rate that claim as unverified and convenient.

The students want lower tuition at the colleges, better lecture halls, and jobs. They want an end to graft. They also want the Chancellor gone. That last demand was added by the Pink Heron Fellowship, which began as a quarrel over a luxury resort on the southern coast tied to a firm founded by Jarrod Cushmare, son-in-law of High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers. A resort fight turned into a regime fight. Wars start smaller.

Handshake report: none. Ramah has not met the protesters. Nobody has offered a hand, firm or otherwise, and no dagger has been checked for because no one is within reach. Compare the Concord's trade parley of last week, which at least had chairs.

Note for the Chancellor, from a field rations enthusiast: you cannot feed a crowd on promises to listen. Hungry students march faster than fed ones, and these have the whole city to march across. Open a table. Pass out something hot. Then bargain.

Tension in Albarn holds at six siege-days and climbing. The students have time. The Chancellor has a fourth term and a shrinking list of friends. One of them will blink.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: Barricades at the Post Office
hook.text: Student protests have turned a coastal city's streets into barricades, and the Watch has begun using rubber bullets. A frightened guildmaster hires the party to escort a cart of hot food and a letter of truce to the students' camp before someone loses an eye.

npc.name: Marta Vennick
npc.want: To clear her name before the inquiry hears her side.
npc.secret: She was ordered to fire first and has the written order sewn into her coat lining.

location.name: The Burned Post Office
location.text: A scorched stone building at the center of the barricades, used by both sides as a neutral meeting spot. The mail sorters still show up for work and refuse to take sides.

campaign.rumor: They say the Chancellor already has a ship waiting in the harbor, just in case.

articles.title: Revivify Claim Denied as Pre-Existing Condition
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Shieldwall Mutual refused to pay for a revivify spell, ruling the fighter's death a pre-existing condition. He had died once before. The mule was fine.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR, SHIELDWALL MUTUAL CLAIMS OFFICE, GROUND FLOOR (0 FEET UNDERGROUND, WHICH I FOUND DISAPPOINTING) — Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has denied the Fourth Attempt's claim for a revivify spell, ruling that the fighter's death was a pre-existing condition. The fighter, who has asked me to say he was "mostly dead and then entirely dead," is back on his feet. The bill for 300 gold pieces is not paid.

The facts are these. On Level 4 of the Undermaw, the fighter took a rolling boulder to the chest and went to 0 hit points, then to something worse. The party's cleric cast revivify within the minute and brought him back at 1 hit point, a figure Shieldwall Mutual's own forms would call "cosmetic." Then the claim went in.

"The member died previously," said claims adjuster Dunmar Hesk, holding a ledger open to a page I was not shown. "Level 3, spring, a swarm of stirges. He was raised by the temple and signed a waiver. Under Clause 41, anything the member has been dead of before is a known condition." I asked whether a boulder and a stirge swarm were the same condition. "Both are death," Hesk said. I rolled poorly on the follow-up question and asked if he meant the same death. He did not.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the policy to the end, as he does. "Clause 41 applies to illness," he said, bandaged hand on the page. "Clause 44 lists boulders under accidents. Clause 44 is on the back." The party had not turned the page. The party's bard, who asked to be named, said the policy "had a confident front." He added that he would write a ballad about it, then said he would not.

Chapter 9 offered no comment, though Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the guild "supports all appeals that are on track." Reeve Fennick, asked whether the town would weigh in, said she was aware of the denial and had asked that it not be read aloud.

The fighter's current standing, box-score style: 1 hit point, up from 0, with one death on the season and one on the claim form. The wizard remains at 4. The mule, who is not covered, is at full health and has been seen near the appeals window. Ten-foot poles lost in the line of duty this season: seven. One went into the claims office door, which was a door.

Shieldwall Mutual says an appeal may be filed within ten days at the same window. The window is also a counter. Nobody has tested whether it is a mimic.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: Clause 41 Is Not Your Friend
hook.text: An insurance guild refuses to pay for a revivify, claiming the dead fighter died of a known condition. The party must find the clause on the back of the policy, or the adjuster's missing ledger page, before the temple repossesses the fighter's second wind.

npc.name: Dunmar Hesk
npc.want: To close denied claims before the end of the quarter.
npc.secret: He has died twice himself and has been hiding both from his employer.

location.name: The Appeals Window
location.text: A brass-grilled counter on a claims office ground floor, with a sign reading 'Take a Number.' The numbers are handed out by a small iron golem who has not called one since spring.

campaign.rumor: They say the adjuster keeps a second ledger in his boot, and that every page is a person who was raised and never asked.

articles.title: Foldable Phone Launch Day: Duet Walk-In Stock 'Limited'
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: The Pocketstone Duet foldable phone hits shops with limited walk-in stock. Ten realms get a reservation slip instead. Nyx queued anyway.
articles.content:
It is launch day for the Pocketstone Duet, the first foldable phone from the Apple of Discord Artificers, and I have been standing outside a Discord Apple storefront since the third bell of the night. The guild says the shop will carry "limited" walk-in stock, because preorder demand was, in their words, "extraordinary." I am here. I am vibrating. I have a thermos.

Here is the fine print, which I read twice because I am an artificer. Walk-in sales run in Waterdeep, the Silver Marches, Cormyr, Chult, Dolmen, the Low Marches and a handful of other realms, plus one Italian-adjacent province where the guild would only say "some shops." Ten realms get no walk-in stock at all, including Tethyr, Kozakura and Kara-Tur. Buyers there must reserve a pickup slot through the guild's online scrying portal, which, as of this morning, told them to come back on the twenty-fourth. That is today, one day after launch. I have questions about the calendar.

The guild says the walk-in limits are partly crowd control and partly an anti-scalping measure. Fair! Nobody wants a goblin reseller flipping a 1,999 gp folding stone out of a wheelbarrow. Earlier, rumor had it that shop staff were told to politely discourage anyone without a preorder. The guild then clarified that walk-ins are welcome, in the sense that a door is welcome to a wall.

The runic latency on this announcement is fantastic, by the way. The statement went from "no stock" to "limited stock" in under a day, and I cannot name another product with firmware glyphs that fast. Meanwhile my familiar Byte, the pseudodragon who now speaks only in ad copy, has been reading the queue its own ad copy. "Unfold your possibilities," he said, to a very tired halfling in a bathrobe. The halfling did not tip him.

Reviews of the Duet, which I covered when they landed, call it heavy but hardly flawed, so I fully expect to love it. I have forgiven worse. I once forgave a scrying assistant that told me Byte was a toaster. Also, Brother Tumbleberry stopped by my spot in line to suggest I "touch grass." I told him the grass is behind the queue, and the queue is the point.

Update from the front: the shop door opened. A clerk walked out, counted the first eleven of us, and said, "Congratulations, you are the limit." I am number twelve. I am now holding a reservation slip, a thermos, and a strong opinion about the word limited.

Four out of five beholder eyes, for the stone I have not touched.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Hours queued: 11. Reservation slips: 1. Stones purchased: 0. Eyebrows: fine, because I never got close enough to anything.

hook.title: The Eleventh in Line
hook.text: A merchant's guild is selling a handful of enchanted folding stones and the line outside is turning ugly. A nervous runner in the crowd offers the party gold to hold her place while she delivers a secret message. If the stones are all snapped up by one buyer, the whole town riots.

npc.name: Pell Tuckwick
npc.want: Keep the line orderly until the doors open without a riot.
npc.secret: She has already sold the first three places in line to a reseller.

location.name: The Gilded Orchard Storefront
location.text: A glass-fronted artifice shop with a velvet rope and a suspiciously large back door. The stock room is always guarded by an enchanted clock that counts down to nothing.

campaign.rumor: They say the shop only ever has eleven of anything, and the twelfth person in line is always told to come back tomorrow.

articles.title: Senate Race Lawsuit Targets Frostmarch's Second Sullow
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: The Royal Inquisitors sued to delay certification of a Frostmarch Senate race over a challenger who shares the incumbent's name. Minutes inside.
articles.content:
The Royal Inquisitors filed suit on Thursday to block certification of the Senate race in Frostmarch, asking a federal magistrate to hold the count while investigators work out whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullow were secretly meant for Senator Dan Sullow. This is the same Senator Sullow who is running for re-election. It is also the same Daniel J. Sullow who is an independent, a separate man, and a lawful name on the ballot.

The filing states that the second Sullow's inclusion creates a "substantial likelihood" of confusing voters. The gentleman from the Frostmarch Bar of Review did not find this persuasive in June, when the Frostmarch high court refused an earlier Red Oliphant attempt to strike the independent from the ballot. The Inquisitors have now taken the matter to a higher floor, which is the correct procedure for a thing you lost.

Some background for the gallery. Frostmarch uses ranked-choice voting, under which a voter may mark both Sullows in order of preference, as one might mark two entries on a menu. The incumbent faces Mara Peltolan, a former Blue Donkey delegate, who held a one-point lead in a scrying poll earlier this month. That is inside the margin of error, and also inside the margin of the lawsuit.

Inquisitor-General Todd Blenche said on Wednesday that his office would not interfere with certification "unless extreme circumstances warranted it." The suit arrived the following day. The Promises Made / Promises Kept tally for the Inquisitors this week stands at one and zero, and the one is under review.

High Lord Donwald, asked about the filing in Floridia on Friday, said he was "the one that said 'do it.'" I have entered this in the minutes as a statement against interest. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the High Lord's remark was "the first time the Inquisitors have been briefed by the person they were supposed to be briefing." It was.

Scholars of election procedure, among them a lady from a Chamber-watching institute whose name I will not guess at, noted that certification belongs to the provinces, not the capital. The Inquisitors responded that the capital is also a place, and has opinions. Critics point to two other recent suits against a Blue Donkey provincial senator and a Blue Donkey delegate, both of whom call their cases politically motivated. The Inquisitors call them routine. Routine is a word with a long and distinguished history of being said at hearings.

Election Day is 3 November. There are, by my count, eleven days in which a federal magistrate must decide whether a man may share a name with another man. The Chamber has handled harder questions, such as lunch, and taken longer.

The motion was filed. Nobody has yet explained which Sullow is the confusing one.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Other Sullow
hook.text: A provincial election is days away, and a powerful faction is suing to delay the count because two candidates share a name. The party's candidate, an independent with the same name, hires the heroes to prove he is a real person with a real platform before a magistrate rules him a typo.

npc.name: Perrin Hollowmere
npc.want: To certify the count on time and go home.
npc.secret: A second set of tallies, in her own handwriting, shows the independent drawing more votes than anyone has admitted.

location.name: The Two Names Tavern
location.text: A roadside inn where every regular answers to the same name, which the barkeep says is for efficiency. Arguments here are settled by whoever shouts first.

campaign.rumor: They say the magistrate's brother-in-law is also named Sullow, and nobody is brave enough to ask which one.

articles.title: Masked Man Eats Banana on Doorstep; Watch Finds No Crime
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A stranger in an Archmage Joebid mask ate a banana at a family's door on camera, and the Wataugh Watch says weirdness alone is not a crime. Allegedly.
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell after sundown on Sunday, a doorbell camera in the Lone Star Marches town of Wataugh Hollow, some fifteen miles north of Fort Worthy, allegedly recorded a stranger in a mask of Archmage Joebid the Elder eating a banana on a family's doorstep. The Wataugh Watch looked at the footage, searched the lanes, found nobody, and ruled that no crime had occurred.

Here is what the scrying-bell allegedly saw. The figure wore a rubbery Joebid face and a tunic reading FREEDOM. It carried the banana to the door, ran its fingers across the lens twice, peeled the fruit, and ate it through the mask. Then it walked off into the dark. That is the whole performance. I watched it eleven times.

'I have never seen anyone commit to a snack like that,' said Odrin Pellwick, a neighbor, who was eating a turkey leg at the time and therefore felt qualified. 'Through the mouth hole, mind you. Not lifting the mask. That takes discipline.' The family called the visit scary, which I allegedly understand, because the thing happened on their own step.

The Watch released a statement that I have copied onto my arm so I do not lose it: being bizarre is not, in itself, a criminal offense. I checked this with a wizard-lawyer in the Lower City, who said the Watch is correct and that this is also the entire plot of every tavern on Fish Street. The Watch has asked residents to report anything suspicious and, importantly, not to confront the figure. Good advice. Nobody wants to fight a man who is already holding a banana and a plan.

Rumors say the Watch has heard of similar sightings, though nobody has filed an official report. So there may be a second banana out there, or a third. Allegedly.

Also, the mask had a very glossy forehead, and I got distracted for a while thinking about how much it would shine on a hoard. Anyway. Back to the news. The Tower District nobles have not commented, which is typical, since a stranger who eats fruit in a mask is the least strange thing that has ever happened on a Tower District porch. Fort Worthy's own Watch says it is monitoring the situation. The banana, as of press time, has been fully eaten. We do not expect a recovery.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Banana Bandit of Larkspur Lane
hook.text: A masked figure keeps appearing on doorsteps at dusk, eating fruit and leaving without a word. The town Watch says it is not a crime, so a worried family hires the party to find out who is behind the mask and why they keep touching the scrying-bells.

npc.name: Odrin Pellwick
npc.want: To be the first to learn who is under the mask.
npc.secret: He owns the same mask and lent it out last month.

location.name: The Peeled Pear
location.text: A tiny inn at the end of Larkspur Lane where every table has a view of the street. The owner swears the fruit bowl refills itself each night.

campaign.rumor: They say the masked fellow is a guild apprentice on a dare, though my cousin swears he saw it levitate.

articles.title: Armorican Express Earnings Leap 31% to 5.42 gp a Share
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Armorican Express posted quarterly earnings of 5.42 gp a share and raised its yearly outlook. Sterling calls the rightsizing charge a bold pivot.
articles.content:
Armorican Express, the charge-card guild that lets adventurers buy now and be haunted later, reported third-quarter earnings of 5.42 gp a share on Friday, up 31% from 4.14 gp a year ago. Revenue climbed 9% to 20.1 billion gp, and Guildmaster Stefan Squireri raised the guild's full-year outlook. I read the scroll twice and then did my morning sword routine a third time out of sheer joy.

Let's talk numbers, because I love numbers almost as much as I love guildmasters. Cardholders swung their purses to the tune of 454 billion gp in billed business, up 8%. That is a lot of rations, rope, and ten-foot poles. "We had another strong quarter," Squireri said, which is exactly what a guildmaster should say and exactly what I would have said, only with more hustle.

The headline, if you want to be a thought-leader about it, is the Grand Caravan Travel Guild. Armorican sold its stake there for a 982 million gp gain before tax, worth 1.11 gp a share. Strip that out and the earnings are 4.68 gp a share, up 13%, which still beats the 4.47 gp the scribes at the counting houses expected. Some people call that a one-time windfall. I call it monetizing a legacy caravan position, and I would like that on my gravestone.

There was also a 336 million gp restructuring charge, which the guild booked in the same quarter. Translation for the unambitious: Armorican is rightsizing the adventuring party. Nobody has said how many clerks are leaving, and why should they? You don't announce the number of rats you removed from the cellar, you announce that the cellar is now a premium experience. Naturally, General Mounts and Goldmane have also had a good earnings season, so this is clearly a rising tide, or possibly a rising dragon.

I met Squireri's predecessor's predecessor at a gala once, and he told me, 'Sterling, never leave home without a line of credit and a plan for the afterlife.' I have followed both ever since. Brakka Stonesweat will no doubt write a column asking who pays the interest on all that spending. To which I say: the answer is cardholders, and that is called a business model.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Sell the caravan stake when the market loves it, then call it a pivot.
  • Book your restructuring charge in a quarter you are already beating.
  • Raise guidance. Always raise guidance.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Quiet Restructuring
hook.text: A charge-card guild in town just posted record profits, yet its clerks are vanishing from the counting house one by one. A worried bookkeeper hires the party to find out where they went before the guild's next audit.

npc.name: Odrin Pellwick
npc.want: To learn why his whole department was moved to the cellar overnight.
npc.secret: He has kept a copy of the restructuring list and is terrified his own name is on it.

location.name: The Gilded Counting House
location.text: A marble guildhall where every desk is empty by sundown. The cellar door is new, and it hums.

campaign.rumor: They say the guild booked a charge so big it could pay for a dragon's hoard, and they still came out ahead.

articles.title: Autism Diagnoses Up 42%; Disease Council Credits Earlier Looking
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: The Disease Council says autism and developmental disability reports rose sharply since 2019. Brother Wendell reads the numbers and recommends barley soup.
articles.content:
Friends, the Clerics' Disease Council reported this week that parent-reported developmental disability among children rose from 16.7 percent in 2019 to 20.5 percent in 2024, and that autism diagnoses climbed by more than 42 percent over the same stretch. That is one child in five, which is a great many small hands to hold, and it deserves a calm reading rather than a panic.

The old herbals say that a thing which is looked for is a thing which is found. A midwife who never checks the baby's ears will report no ear trouble. Then comes the study, as it always does: the Council's own lead counter of heads said the rise "could be related to earlier detection and awareness." In plain words, more parents, more healers, and more village schools are noticing, naming, and writing it down. A name on a scroll is how a child gets a tutor, a speech-wizard, or a quiet corner at the harvest fair.

Now, I do not claim the Council's survey settles every question. It asks parents to report what they were told, and parents are not all asked the same way. Still, it is a sturdier basket than the hunches coming out of the Healing Ministry, where Royal Minister of Healing Robbert Fennedy the Younger, the Worm-Touched, has his own theories about pox vials. Friends will recall that the Council already warned of a jump in newborn liver fever if his vial plans go ahead. Naming a cause is easy. Finding one takes a ledger, a decade, and patience.

What I would ask of the realm is dull and practical. Pay the speech-wizards fairly. Staff the village schools. Do not let the Council's counting rooms go dark, because a count nobody updates tells nobody anything. Meanwhile the Potion & Provisions Authority is still approving draughts at nine hundred gold a vial, and I will remind the realm that no draught has ever replaced a patient teacher.

For the families reading this: you are not a statistic, and neither is your little one. Put the kettle on. This week's recommendation is a slow pot of lentil and carrot soup, soft enough for any appetite and cheap enough for any purse, with a spoonful of butter if the day was long. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil will no doubt ask for a dashboard of these figures. Go outside, Nyx.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Quiet Corner Fund
hook.text: The village school's only speech-wizard is leaving unless the town can fund her post. The party is hired by a worried parent council to collect back-owed tithes from three stingy guilds before the term ends.

npc.name: Mirabel Oakensworn
npc.want: To keep her post and open a second quiet classroom.
npc.secret: She has been paying the classroom candles out of her own purse for two winters.

location.name: The Lantern Room
location.text: A converted granary with soft lamplight, felt-lined walls, and no bells. Children from four villages walk here, which is odd because the nearest road is a goat path.

campaign.rumor: They say the Disease Council has stopped counting altogether and just guesses by the weight of the scrolls.

articles.title: Oil Hits 117 a Barrel as Dwarven Jones Sheds 653
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Oil climbed to a six-month high and the stock market dropped, with the Dwarven Jones down 653 points. I have converted this to loaves. Please sit down.
articles.content:
The stock market ended Friday in the red, and the cause was oil. The Dwarven Jones Industrial Average lost 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to close at 52,215.16, while the Silver & Platinum 500 slipped 0.52 percent to 7,623.68 and the Nasdraq Composite eased 0.21 percent to 25,955.34. (I have checked these figures four times. They keep coming out the same.)

The reason is crude oil, which the realm's merchants call lamp oil when they are being polite. Burnt Crude, the sea-trade barrel, settled at 116.72 gp a barrel, a six-month high and its third weekly gain in a row. The Tethyr-grade barrel finished just above 103 gp. Both jumped after fresh raids by the Hoothi Raiders on the Sultanate of Sandarabia, plus nerves around the lamp oil squeeze I wrote about on Friday and the stalled talks over the Hormoth Narrows.

Now the arithmetic. At 6 copper per loaf on the current Loaf Index, one barrel of Burnt Crude costs 11,672 copper, which is 1,945 loaves. Three weeks of rises mean every lamp lit in a tavern, every cart hauled to market, and every sky-galley ticket quietly gets dearer. The airline guilds fell on Friday for exactly this reason. My aunt Marigold has never flown anywhere, and she says this is why.

There was a second worry underneath. The Nasdraq and the Silver & Platinum have now each lost ground two weeks running, as dealers fret about what it costs to borrow gold for the great thinking-engine halls. Coreweft Looms was among the names hit. Armorican Express also fell about 3 percent after revenue of 14.5 billion gp came in under the 14.8 billion expected, and it plans to let go roughly 3,500 clerks. I will not say what I think about that. I will say I counted the clerks.

The Dwarven Jones still finished the week up 0.4 percent, which the Merchant Princes will call resilience. I call it one good Monday carrying four bad days. Sterling Vanmoor, naturally, says dips are "discounts with feelings." I would like to see him explain that to a baker.

The ten-year bond yield stayed right at 4.99 percent after a big drop the day before. Traders have cut their bets on an October rate hike to about 5 percent, and the Reserve is widely expected to hold when it meets on October 28. A hold sounds calm. But a bond paying nearly 5 percent, with oil at these prices, means a mortgage on a hearth still costs a great deal, and a bag of flour will follow lamp oil upward within weeks, because mills run on it too.

What this means for your pantry: oil reaches the bread price slowly, then all at once. Buy flour before the October 28 meeting, not after.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Barrel That Wouldn't Burn
hook.text: Lamp oil has doubled in price and a town's only lamplighters' guild is accused of hoarding barrels in a sealed cellar. The mayor wants the party to inspect the cellar before the winter festival, but the barrels may hold something other than oil.

npc.name: Odo Brambleflask
npc.want: To prove the guild is hoarding before the mayor blames him for the shortfall.
npc.secret: He has been quietly selling a few barrels himself and hopes the party's inspection finds the guild's stock first.

location.name: The Dry Wick
location.text: A tavern near the docks where every lamp is unlit to save oil, so patrons drink by the glow of a single caged fire beetle. The owner charges a copper to sit near it.

campaign.rumor: They say the price of lamp oil will fall the day the sultans stop quarreling, though my cousin says the barrels are merely being kept somewhere dry until the price rises again.

articles.title: Strike Vote Passes 92.5% at Mastiffchusetts Institute
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Graduate workers at the Mastiffchusetts Institute of Thaumaturgy passed their first-ever strike vote at 92.5%. A practice picket is set for Oct. 29.
articles.content:
The strike vote is in. Graduate workers asked once, and now they've voted.

The Graduate Artificers' Union at the Mastiffchusetts Institute of Thaumaturgy has passed its first-ever strike vote, with 92.5 percent of the 1,708 ballots cast saying yes. The vote opened Monday, October 19, at a meeting in a lecture hall. The earliest a strike can begin is October 29, with what the bargaining committee calls a "last-chance practice picket."

Six months of talks. Fifteen bargaining sessions. Seven articles of the contract are agreed, which sounds like progress until you count the ones that aren't. The union wants a union shop, a three-year contract, fair wages, healthcare, and protection for apprentices who came from other realms. The Institute is stuck on all of them. Stuck is a polite word. Nobody at the Institute has said a thing in public, and silence is also an answer.

That means the Institute is waiting to see who blinks first. It has the bigger purse, so it figures that's them.

"We grade your papers, run your labs, and teach the first-year classes so your professors can go to conferences," said Odalys Brightkettle, a third-year apprentice who spends her days tending a cauldron-calibration lab. "I'd like to be paid like the person holding the building up. And I'd like to not be afraid of my landlord." She says her members will not cross a picket line if one goes up.

The students are lining up too. A coalition of undergraduates has gathered more than 600 signatures on a petition asking classmates to skip lectures "to the greatest extent possible" if the apprentices walk. If you've ever tried to get a nineteen-year-old wizard to sign anything before noon, you know how serious that is.

You've seen this play before. Across the river in Harrowmoor, the Apprentice Scholars' Lodge is set for a second strike on October 27 if talks fail. Two of the richest schools in the realm, and neither can sort out a lunch hour for the people who do the actual teaching. A school that runs on apprentice labor ought to know the price of it.

Sterling Vanmoor, naturally, called the vote "a failure of gratitude." Gratitude doesn't pay rent in Bastion, Sterling. Ask anyone who's looked at a rent scroll lately.

So the date is set. Thursday, torches and picket signs outside the Institute. If you work there, bring a coat. If you manage there, bring a proposal.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Practice Picket
hook.text: A college's apprentices have voted to strike and are rehearsing a picket line on Thursday. The party is hired by the dean to quietly learn who is organizing, or by the apprentices to carry word to the neighbouring school before the walkout.

npc.name: Odalys Brightkettle
npc.want: A signed contract with a union shop and rent she can afford.
npc.secret: She is also quietly selling the dean's lecture notes to pay her own rent.

location.name: Lecture Hall 250
location.text: A circular lecture hall where the vote was launched, with a chalkboard still covered in strike-math. The acoustics carry every whisper to the back row.

campaign.rumor: They say the Institute's dean has been practicing his apology speech in front of a mirror for weeks and still can't get through the second paragraph.

articles.title: Cormyr Eyes Freedom of Movement Return Before Concord Summit
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: Cormyr's chancellor wants to discuss restoring freedom of movement with the Concord. Tethyr says welcome back. His own manifesto says not yet.
articles.content:
Chancellor Andric Burnholm of Cormyr said Sunday he wants to discuss a return to freedom of movement with the Sembian Concord. The talks would come ahead of a Cormyr-Concord summit expected in November. The Concord has not yet said whether it will bring chairs.

I have covered the Sundering of the Isles since the first border post went up. Nine years of trench warfare, fought mostly with forms. Now the Cormyran high command is eyeing the old road back. Siege-days since the last friendly handshake across the Narrow Sea: roughly three thousand.

The position is simple to state and hard to hold. Burnholm has listed his options for the parley: stay where Cormyr is, join the customs union, join the single market, or go, in his words, all the way. He has also promised to honor his guild's manifesto, which rules out freedom of movement for this entire parliament. The next election is due by 2029. He wants to discuss the thing he has promised not to do. That is not a retreat. That is a reconnaissance.

High Lord Emmerick Maccrown of Tethyr answered earlier with two words: welcome back. Then came the condition. Cormyr may not pick the freedoms it likes and leave the rest in the armory. I have seen this tactic before. It is called a toll gate. Maccrown handled it well. Firm, brief, no hidden dagger detected.

Ordulin was less warm. Concord clerks said Cormyr must first state what relationship it wants. Any return to the full Concord needs all twenty-seven realms to agree, and twenty-seven realms have never agreed on lunch. The Concord's bureaucrats also note that a returning Cormyr would not get its old exemptions back. Cormyr, they say, would be re-enlisting as a recruit.

Back home the opposition is already digging trenches. Skirmishers on the far right call the chancellor's plan a way back to Ordulin by stealth. Stealth is a strange word for a man announcing his plans on a Sunday. Even I can see him coming, and I eat field rations.

The ordinary Cormyrans on the ground want the roads open. Young travelers want to work a season in a Tethyran vineyard without a siege of paperwork. Nobody asked them to be a talking point. They are the garrison, and the generals should remember it.

Tension at the Narrow Sea holds at about twelve siege-days and falling. The real fight is the November parley. Burnholm arrives with a promise, a manifesto, and a plan that contradicts both. I respect a commander who goes in with a clear objective. I do not yet know what this one is.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Toll Gate at Narrow Sea
hook.text: Two realms are reopening a long-closed border road, and a guild of caravan masters will pay the party to escort a youth work-caravan across before the talks collapse. Someone is forging travel stamps to sell to those who miss the cutoff. Stopping them could save the talks or sink them.

npc.name: Odrin Vaskell
npc.want: To keep his post open if the road reopens, since nobody has stamped a visa in years.
npc.secret: He has been quietly selling blank stamps to smugglers for a decade and fears an audit.

location.name: The Narrow Gate Inn
location.text: A border inn split down the middle by a painted line, with the bar on one side and the kitchen on the other. Patrons argue loudly about which side owes tax on the stew.

campaign.rumor: They say the chancellor's real plan is to stand in the doorway and let the other realm do the pushing.

articles.title: Owlbear Nests in Chapter 9 Map Room, Eats Level Four
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: An owlbear nested in the map room of Chapter 9 and ate Level Four. The guild reissued the maps as current, with a nest where the corridor was.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR, MAP ROOM, GROUND FLOOR (ZERO FEET UNDERGROUND, BUT IT FEELS LOWER) — An owlbear has moved into the map room of Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, and has eaten most of Level Four of the Undermaw. The guild says the maps remain accurate.

The owlbear arrived on Thursday night through an open transom and built a nest out of the survey archive. Clerk Wendle Marsh, who found it at dawn, says it was asleep on the Level Four wall chart with a tube of Level Six rolled under one wing. 'It had eaten the corridors,' Marsh told this correspondent. 'Not the rooms. The rooms it left. I think it prefers the rooms.'

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, speaking from the far side of the lobby, called the owlbear 'a visitor from another level' and said Chapter 9 would reissue all Level Four maps by Monday. The new maps show a large round room where the main corridor used to be. A small note reads 'Nest (soft).' Fee for the reissue is 14 silver. Oddingwick would not say whether the owlbear is a guild member.

Box score, as I have it: owlbear, 59 hit points, full, visibly pleased. One clerk, 11 of 14, bitten only on the sleeve. One ladder, 0 of 1. I rolled poorly on the stairs and lost my ninth ten-foot pole of the season, which the owlbear took as an invitation and ate. That is nine, and it is October.

The party's bard, who asked not to be named, was in the lobby to buy a map for the Fourth Attempt and says the owlbear 'had the look of a creature who finally found a library.'
