That's 12.5% of the goal, which makes it perfectly exclusive. Nobody is sitting on an overstocked lot of Ex-Sixty Wains. You can't say that about some other guilds I could name.

The 2,500 positions follow an earlier round of 3,000, which makes this a cadence, not a crisis. Workers will be phased out by mid-2027, so everyone gets a long runway to update their scrolls. The guild must also find another 5 billion gp in savings, though it has over 30 billion gp in the vault. That's what I call dry powder. When I met Guildmaster Jeff Bezoar at a gala, he told me, "Sterling, a vault is just a hoard with good PR." I wrote that on my forearm.

Also, next year Klaus Zellmaer, formerly of Skodra, takes the chair. A fresh pair of hands, a fresh round of cuts, and a fresh slide deck. Succession planning is the sexiest kind of planning. I'm told the owners at Geelyx Holdings are thrilled, though I have not asked them and do not intend to. Some questions are better left in the pipeline. My rival Brakka Stonesweat will no doubt write a column about the 2,500 families. I say they're 2,500 future founders.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A record low is also a record. Lead with that.
  • If you lose five times the forecast, you have outperformed the forecast at losing.
  • Build 12.5% of your target. Call it scarcity.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Wagon Works Walkout
hook.text: A wainwright guild has fired 2,500 workers and withdrawn its forecasts, and the laid-off foremen are quietly selling blueprints for its flagship wagon. A rival merchant wants the party to buy them first before the plans leave town.

npc.name: Ingrid Halvarsen
npc.want: To get severance pay for her whole crew before the guild seals the books.
npc.secret: She has a copy of the wagon's flawed axle designs and knows why only a few thousand were built.

location.name: The Idle Axle
location.text: A tavern near the wagon works where laid-off carpenters trade rumors. Every table is a half-built wagon, and the owner insists it's an exclusive limited run.

campaign.rumor: They say the guild has thirty million in the vault and not one spare copper for the workers, and the new chair is bringing his own accountants.

articles.title: Outbreak Doubles Last Year's Total: 4,588 Red-Spot Cases
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: The Disease Council counts 4,588 red-spot fever cases in Waterdeep, double last year. Brother Wendell asks friends to please just get the vial.
articles.content:
Friends, the Clerics' Disease Council reports 4,588 confirmed cases of red-spot fever in Waterdeep this year as of October 22, more than double the whole of last year. It is the worst outbreak season the realm has seen since 1991, and the Sylvanpenn Marches alone have logged 1,360 cases across 44 counties.

I last wrote about the 4,080 mark a few weeks ago, and I confess I hoped we had seen the worst of it. The old herbals say a fever like this rides the air for two hours after the sick person has left the room, which means a single sneeze in a tavern can outlast the sneezer, the bard, and one round of mulled cider. Nine in ten folk who have not had the vial and walk into that room will catch it. The Council says 96 in every 100 cases this year were among the unvaccinated, or folk whose vaccination nobody could find a record of, which is a different kind of problem.

The Council also counts 43 new outbreaks. I picture each one as a little red flag on a map, and the map now looks like a hedgehog. The Sylvanpenn Marches report 258 hospital stays, and clerics there tell me they have started keeping spare cots in the chapel and, I am told, in the chapel's other chapel.

Now for the good news, because there is always some. Two doses of the pox-vial are nearly 97 in 100 effective, and Sylvanpenn gave out more than 39,000 of them in the first three weeks of October, well above the usual 25,000 for a whole month. Somebody out there is listening. One halfling apothecary in Sylvanpenn told me the queue outside her shop wound past the cheesemonger, around the well, and into the next barony, where a very confused baron joined it just to be polite.

What I will not do, friends, is tell you soup cures red-spot fever. It does not. Soup is for the sick room, for the sleepless, for the neighbour who cannot cook this week. The vial is for the fever. Before the vial arrived in the realm, three to four million folk caught it every year, and a normal year now sees fewer than two hundred. That is the finest bargain any cleric has ever offered, and it costs far less than the nine hundred gold some potion-makers ask for a healing draught.

So check your family's scrolls, friends. If a record is missing, ask your village cleric, and if you are travelling, ask before you go rather than after you sneeze. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says the whole thing could be tracked better with a scrying app. Perhaps so, Nyx, but first go outside and knock on a neighbour's door to ask if they are boosted.

This week's soup is chicken and rice, thin and salty, for whoever you are looking after.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Missing Vial Ledger
hook.text: A fever of red spots is running through the district, and the village cleric cannot find vaccination records for half the children. Someone must track down the scattered ledgers before the next market day packs the square.

npc.name: Odette Marrowgrass
npc.want: To get every family's vial records found and up to date before market day.
npc.secret: She lost the parish ledger herself, left it in a tavern, and has told no one.

location.name: The Chapel of Two Chapels
location.text: A small shrine so overrun with cots that the cleric built a second chapel beside it. The second one is already half full.

campaign.rumor: They say the cheesemonger's queue is only that long because the baker started handing out free rolls to anyone who shows a vial scar.

articles.title: Bag of Holding Hides 40,000 Flour Sacks; Bread Doubles
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: A Brindlemoor miller stored 40,000 flour sacks in one bag of holding, and the price of bread doubled in a week. Barnaby has checked the math. Four times.
articles.content:
A Brindlemoor miller named Odo Pennyfeather has been found to have stored 40,000 sacks of flour inside a single bag of holding, and the town's bread price doubled in a week as a result. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor ordered the bag opened on Monday morning, with a bucket brigade standing by.

The arithmetic is simple, which is why it frightens me. (I have checked it four times.) A loaf cost two copper pieces last tenday and four this tenday, so the Loaf Index, my own humble measure, has gone from 1.00 to 2.00. Forty thousand sacks at roughly sixty loaves each is 2.4 million loaves, enough to feed the town for eleven weeks. Mr. Pennyfeather is not selling any of it.

Mr. Pennyfeather says he is simply being prudent. "Prices rise in autumn," he told reporters outside his mill. "I put the flour somewhere safe until they do." When asked whether his own hoarding was the reason prices were rising, he said the market would sort itself out. I had to sit down.

The economics underneath are plain enough. When a seller takes goods off the shelves and waits, the goods left are scarcer, and scarce flour costs more, so the miller's guess about autumn comes true because he made it come true. A bag of holding makes this very cheap to do, since forty thousand sacks weigh the same as fifteen. A wagon of that size would have been noticed. A belt pouch was not.

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule says her kitchen is down to one loaf a day, which she cuts into eight and serves with an apology. "I've fed gelatinous cubes cheaper," she said. Inspector Corwin Tallowby, no relation to me (I have asked), has filed the hoard under cellar matters, which it is not.

Reeve Fennick's order takes effect Monday. The bag may be opened only by its owner, and only over a dry floor with town guards present, because a bag of holding that is torn or turned inside out sends its contents to another plane. Nobody wants forty thousand sacks of flour spilled across the Astral Sea. Master Millwright Dunstan Roe estimates the town guards will need two days to carry it all out.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says the miller and she have more in common than I would like, which is a thing she should not have said. A boot, however, holds a few coins. A bag of holding holds a barony's supper.

What this means for your pantry: buy a sack now, check your neighbor's belt pouch, and do not trust anyone who says it will sort itself out.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Bottomless Pantry
hook.text: A miller has hidden a town's worth of grain in a bag of holding, and bread prices are climbing. The mayor wants the party to escort the bag open without tearing it, while the miller's rivals would rather it vanish.

npc.name: Odo Pennyfeather
npc.want: To sell his flour only when prices peak.
npc.secret: The bag has a small tear, and he knows it could spill at any time.

location.name: The Pennyfeather Mill
location.text: A watermill with a wheel that has not turned in a tenday. The cellar is spotless and empty, which no one has explained.

campaign.rumor: They say the miller's bag goes somewhere much deeper than anyone thinks, and there's a baker living in it.

articles.title: Kobolds Vote 31-2 to Unionize Over Scrip Pay at Chapter 9
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Thirty-three kobold trap-resetters voted 31 to 2 to form a union. Chapter 9 pays them in scrip that only buys Chapter 9 goods.
articles.content:
The kobolds want real coin.

Thirty-three kobold trap-resetters who rebuild the pits, darts and swinging blades of the Undermaw voted 31 to 2 last night to form a union. The vote was held in a cellar on Tanner's Row, after shift, over a shared pot of stew. Their employer, Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, pays them in 'delve scrip.' It is good at the Chapter 9 map shop, the Chapter 9 rope counter and the Chapter 9 canteen. It is good nowhere else.

The guild's pay notice calls this 'a closed-loop compensation ecosystem.' That means they pay you in tokens and then sell you your own dinner.

'I reset the pit on Level Two forty times a tenday,' said Krix Dusktail, a trap-resetter for six years. 'Some adventurer falls in it, I climb down, I dig out the adventurer, I put the spikes back. They pay me in a coupon for a map I already know by heart.'

The arithmetic is worse than the coupon. The canteen charges scrip at a rate of three to the copper, but the scrip pays out at four to the copper. Nobody at Chapter 9 could explain the difference. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the rate was 'on track' and 'a feature.' He added that kobolds enjoy the canteen's turnip pie. Krix says nobody enjoys it. 'I eat it. That's different.'

The kobolds are also short a chair. Resetters work crouched in the dark, because the guild's sizing chart says 'a kobold is naturally low.' Zeb Cindermaw, who rebuilds the dart wall on Level Four, said his knees stop working around the seventh tenday of every season. 'Natural,' said Zeb. 'Like my rent.'

Their demands are modest. Wages in silver, paid on the last day of the tenday. A real lunch break, with a bench. And a shop steward who answers to the kobolds, not to the guild. They've asked Ansel Pottage, who has read more guild contracts than anyone alive, to help them draft the first one. Pottage said he would read the scrip notice aloud at the hearing, which should take about a minute and a half. 'It's very short,' he said. 'That's the problem with it.'

Reeve Fennick said the town is 'aware of the kobolds' and will review the vote. Oddingwick said Chapter 9 'respects workers' voices' and plans to answer the union with a new scrip, in a different color.

The two kobolds who voted no told a reporter they like the canteen. Both then asked, quietly, whether the stew from the cellar could be served again next week.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Scrip Ledger
hook.text: A union of kobold trap-resetters is about to strike, and the local guild has locked its books to hide a skimmed exchange rate. The party is hired to retrieve the ledger from the guild's canteen cellar before the union's first hearing.

npc.name: Krix Dusktail
npc.want: Silver wages paid in real coin on the last day of the tenday.
npc.secret: She has a copy of the guild's exchange-rate ledger hidden inside a pit she resets herself.

location.name: The Chapter Canteen
location.text: A low-ceilinged hall that serves turnip pie and sells every adventurer's supplies at triple the scrip rate. The cellar below is oddly warm, and the cook insists it's the stove.

campaign.rumor: Folk say the scrip is printed on the same press as the permits, and that the press has been running at night.

articles.title: Ghost Ship Docks in Varnholt; Customs Demands a Visa
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: A ghost ship drifted into a Varnholt harbor on Sixthday. Varnholt wants a visa, the Pellam Isles want it back, and the parley is on day two.
articles.content:
A ghost ship drifted into the harbor at Saltreach, Varnholt, on Sixthday, and customs has refused to let its crew come ashore without a visa. The Pellam Isles say the ship, the Gannet's Regret, has been theirs for ninety years and its crew are Pellam subjects. The crew are dead, which neither side disputes.

The parley opened on the quay at dawn. Harbormaster Ilsabet Corvane of Varnholt sat on a barrel. Envoy Dorrin Vask of the Pellam Isles sat on a coil of rope and kept moving it toward her side. The handshake lasted two seconds, and Vask's hand passed through hers on the second. No hidden dagger detected. No hand either.

Varnholt's position is plain. A ship that enters harbor owes a berth fee of six silver pieces a night, and an undead crew owes the same as a living one. The Pellam Isles answer that a ship with no living passengers has no passengers, and a berth fee is a levy on passengers. Corvane replied that the ghosts have been seen eating at the harbor tavern. Vask said they were only standing near the food.

Tension holds at roughly nine siege-days. The harbor is closed to anything with a hull. Eleven merchant crews are anchored outside, and the captain of a spice barge told me he would rather pay a fee to anyone, anywhere, than wait another night. I take that as a vote for the fee. Nobody asked the dead for a vote, since the Varnholt charter says they cannot cast one.

Corvane has ruled that the ghost captain, a tall figure who answers to "Captain", may sign for the ship. The captain signed. The ink faded in an hour, which Varnholt reads as a breach of contract and the Pellam Isles read as a drafting error on Varnholt's side. Vask asked for the signature to be witnessed by a cleric. A cleric was brought and refused to go near the form.

A press release from the Varnholt travel board arrived at noon. It announced a "haunted harbor experience package" at four gold pieces a night, with the ghosts as the featured attraction. I will not describe it further. The crew of the Gannet's Regret read it from the rail and went below, which I count as the first honest reaction at this parley.

A field ration of hard cheese and dried plum went around the quay at dusk. The harbor militia ate. The envoys watched. The ghosts looked away, which is more manners than I have seen in some summits.

The parley resumes at sunrise. The ship stays where it is, and the berth fee keeps adding up. Somebody will lose tomorrow. It will not be the dead.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Visa for the Dead
hook.text: A ghost ship has docked at a trade port and both its home isle and the harbor claim it, with a dozen merchant ships stuck waiting offshore. The harbormaster will pay the party to find out why the ship came in at all, and whether the crew wants something done.

npc.name: Ilsabet Corvane
npc.want: To clear the harbor without losing the berth fees or her post.
npc.secret: She recognizes the ghost captain as her grandfather, and has told no one.

location.name: The Drowned Gannet
location.text: A harbor tavern with a back room that floods at high tide and has never smelled of salt. The ghosts stand in it every night, close to the fire.

campaign.rumor: They say the ghost crew did not drift in by chance and are looking for the one who sold their ship out from under them.

articles.title: Ogre Hired to Hold Door Demands Hazard Pay
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: An ogre hired to hold a door for an adventuring party for six hours filed for hazard pay at Chapter 9. The door, he notes, held back.
articles.content:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2, OUTSIDE THE DOOR — An ogre hired to hold a door for the Fourth Attempt has filed for hazard pay with Chapter 9, after holding it for six hours while something on the far side pushed. The ogre, Brund, was engaged at the standard door-holding rate of four silver a shift. He says the standard rate assumes a door that does not push back.

The box score: Brund started at full hit points and finished at 31 of 59. The door finished at 3 of 18. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the party was 'inside, having a lovely time.' They were looting the room beyond. Brund was not offered a share, a stool, or a word of thanks, which I note as someone who has been told to hold the door and would rather not discuss it.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, took the case within the hour. Pottage is the man who won hazard pay for mimics, and he read the ruling aloud to the hall. It says a hireling is owed hazard pay whenever the thing he stands beside is trying to eat him. 'The door was not trying to eat him,' Pottage said. 'The door was only the thing between him and what was. I would call that closer.'

Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who hears these matters, asked whether the ogre had been bitten, clawed, or otherwise touched. Brund said he had been leaned on. Brackenmoor, who carries a ladle in memory of the mimic, said that was a new category and she would need a minute. The minute has run to two days.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick says Chapter 9 'welcomes the clarification' and that door-holding remains 'on track' as a non-hazardous duty. Asked what was on the other side of the door, he said it was a visitor from another level. Asked which level, he said the matter was soft. By my count that is the fourth thing he has called soft this month.

The party disagrees with Brund, mildly. The fighter, at 14 hit points, says the door was 'a good door' and that nobody told Brund to hold it for six hours. Pottage notes the contract says 'hold until relieved,' and that no one relieved him. Brund was not relieved. He was forgotten, which the contract does not cover and which Pottage is now trying to have added.

Brund, for his part, asks little. He wants hazard rate for the shift, a stool on future delves, and the door, which he has become attached to. He has named it. I rolled poorly and did not catch the name. I did lose my seventh ten-foot pole of the season prodding the thing on the other side, which pushed back.

Brackenmoor will rule at the next sitting. In the meantime the door is being held by two junior hirelings on a rotation, at hazard rate, by informal agreement. Nobody has written that down. Pottage is writing it down.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: The Door That Pushed Back
hook.text: A hireling ogre has held a dungeon door shut for hours against something pushing from the other side, and the party that hired him went in through a different way. Someone must relieve him before the door gives, and learn what is pushing.

npc.name: Brund Haskel
npc.want: Hazard pay, a stool, and to keep his door.
npc.secret: He has been bracing against something that has stopped pushing, and he is afraid to let go and find out why.

location.name: The Held Door
location.text: A reinforced oak door at the end of a ten-foot corridor, scored with claw marks on the inside only. A stool and a ledger of shifts sit beside it.

campaign.rumor: They say the thing behind the door isn't pushing anymore, it's leaning, and it's very patient.

articles.title: Crystal Ball Launches at 40 gp, Future Costs Extra
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Lumenwick's new Seer crystal ball hit Brindlemoor shelves at 40 gp, with the future locked behind a monthly fee. Nyx tested it. Four eyes.
articles.content:
The Lumenwick Seer, a new crystal ball from Lumenwick Glassworks, went on sale in Brindlemoor this morning for 40 gp. The catch is a subscription: the ball shows you the present for free, and the future costs 6 gp a month. I queued overnight outside the Tanner's Row shop and I regret nothing!

Unboxing was flawless. The glass is clear, the stand is walnut, and the firmware glyph on the base lit up the second I touched it. Runic latency is nearly zero. Ask it where your keys are and it answers before you finish the question. (Under the cat. Always under the cat.)

Then I asked about tomorrow. The Seer showed me a hazy gray fog and a small banner: "Unlock the Foresight tier to see what happens next!" I did not unlock it. I would like it noted that I resisted for almost eleven minutes, which for me is a personal best on subscription fees, which I hate.

The free tier, it turns out, has ads. Mid-vision, an imp in a tiny waistcoat appeared in the glass and offered me a deal on cellar insurance. Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, answered it directly. "Foresight. See tomorrow, today." The imp left looking uneasy. I think they were rivals.

A Lumenwick spokesman, Odo Pennywhistle, said the pricing is "a simple, transparent ladder" and that the ad imps are "contractors, not staff." Asked whether the tier that lets you see your own future also shows you the cancellation page, he said it does, eventually, "in the order events actually occur." I tried it. In my vision I cancel on a Thursday, eleven weeks from now, after being asked three times whether I am sure.

Mana throughput is the one real problem. The Seer draws power from whatever is nearby, and that was my candle, my kettle, and, briefly, Byte. Byte is fine, but now glows a little and has started using the word "synergy." Brother Tumbleberry, whose column this week tells readers to put down the crystal ball and touch grass, has not tried it, which I feel shows.

Verdict: gorgeous hardware, a present that is always visible, and a future available in monthly installments. I have already paid for the Foresight tier. I am told that I will cancel it, but I do not yet know how I feel about that. Four out of five beholder eyes.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Subscriptions sustained: 1. Imps argued with: 1. Familiars glowing: 1. Eyebrows: pending, but I foresaw them fine.

hook.title: The Foresight Subscription
hook.text: A shop in town sells crystal balls whose visions of tomorrow are sold by subscription, and customers are quietly being shown futures that rewrite themselves when they cancel. Hosea Tarn, who runs the shop, will pay the party to find out who is editing the visions before the shop is shut down.

npc.name: Hosea Tarn
npc.want: To keep his shop open and find who is tampering with his customers' visions.
npc.secret: He has been selling the balls without checking the ad imps' contracts, and one contract gives the imps ownership of every vision.

location.name: The Glass Ledger
location.text: A narrow shop with a hundred crystal balls on its shelves, each showing a slightly different version of the same afternoon. The back room is full of tiny waistcoats.

campaign.rumor: They say the people who cancel the Foresight tier all wake up a day older than they should be.

articles.title: Owlbear Leash Ordinance Passes 5-4 in Brindlemoor
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: Brindlemoor's Burgess Council passed an owlbear leash ordinance 5-4 after nine hours. The owlbear in the gallery says it will be reviewing the text.
articles.content:
The Burgess Council of Brindlemoor passed Ordinance 41, the owlbear leash ordinance, by a vote of five to four on Tuesday night. It requires any owlbear within the town walls to be restrained by a leash of no more than twelve feet. The ordinance is six lines long. Debate on it ran nine hours.

The session was called for the second bell and began at the fourth, after the gentleman from Tanner's Row finished a speech about starting on time. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor presided and reminded the chamber twice that the bill concerned leashes. It then concerned, in order, the price of rope, the dignity of the owlbear, the dignity of the council, and a cousin of the lady from the Lower Ward who was once startled by a hen.

The central difficulty was the definition. The first draft said a leash must be "sufficient to restrain." The lady from the Smithy Quarter asked sufficient for what, and the clerk, after a pause, said an owlbear. The amendment to define an owlbear as "a creature with the head of an owl and the body of a bear" failed on the grounds that this described the owlbear and also, the gentleman from the Tannery noted, several members.

The owlbear in question, a resident of the Millrace district named Brindle, attended the entire session from the gallery and ate two benches. Asked for comment afterward, it made a sound the clerk recorded as "a low hooting remark, possibly procedural." Its handler, a baker named Hesper Doulby, said Brindle had no objection to a leash in principle but would like it noted that the council has no leash of its own.

The vote itself was brief. Four members opposed it, citing rope costs. Five supported it, citing a general feeling. By my count this brings the session's Promises Made to fourteen, among them a pledge to "review the ordinance in a tenday," and Promises Kept to the one about the benches, which were replaced at public expense.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the rope contract had been settled before the debate began. The supplier is the brother-in-law of the gentleman from the Tannery, who voted no. This is, so far as I can determine, the only consistent thing about the evening.

Enforcement falls to the town constables, who say they have neither rope nor volunteers. Fennick told the gallery, "We are aware of the owlbear," and adjourned at the thirteenth bell. The ordinance takes effect at the next new moon. The council has not yet decided who will hold the other end.

The motion carried. Nobody read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Other End of the Leash
hook.text: A new town ordinance requires an owlbear to be leashed within the walls, but no one will hold the rope. The mayor will pay the party to find a volunteer, or a very strong post, before the next new moon.

npc.name: Hesper Doulby
npc.want: To keep her owlbear Brindle legal without anyone getting a rope near its beak.
npc.secret: Brindle was a gift from a smuggler, and Hesper has no papers for it.

location.name: The Millrace Bakery
location.text: A flour-dusted bakery on the river edge with a reinforced back stable. The loaves are excellent and the walls bear claw marks at exactly owlbear height.

campaign.rumor: They say the rope contract went to the councilman's brother-in-law, and that the rope is mostly string.

articles.title: Swarm of Ravens Strips 212 Buttons Off Constabulary
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A swarm of ravens stole 212 brass buttons from the Constabulary's drying uniforms on Fish Street. Skritch has the scoop, and a button. Allegedly.
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell before dawn, a swarm of ravens allegedly descended on the Constabulary's laundry line on Fish Street and stole 212 brass buttons off 31 dress uniforms. The Constabulary confirms the buttons are gone, the birds are gone, and the trousers are, in the words of Sergeant Orla Pennick, "a matter of morale."

Morning muster was held anyway. Eleven constables reported for duty holding their belts with one hand and their halberds with the other. "I saluted with my knee," said Sergeant Pennick. "It is not in the manual, but neither are ravens."

Witnesses say the swarm worked in perfect order. Tobin Fley, a fishmonger who was gutting a sturgeon at the time, saw the birds line up on the rope, snip the thread with their beaks, and fly off in a spiral. "Very professional," Fley said. "They took the buttons and left the fish. I have never felt so insulted."

The Constabulary has opened an inquiry. Its first lead was a pigeon, which Skritch, personally and allegedly, endorses, because pigeons are guilty of something every day and nobody ever checks. The Constabulary ruled the pigeon out when it was found asleep on a ledge with no buttons and no alibi, which the Constabulary says is the same thing.

The ravens were last seen over the roofs of Tanner's Row, where a nest was found with 140 buttons braided into the lining. Also there was a really beautiful brass lantern hook nearby, with a little curl at the end, and Skritch would like it known that he did not touch it. He did look at it for a while. Anyway. The nest sits eleven floors up a chimney and is allegedly guarded by a very cross crow.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick has been asked whether the town will pay for replacements. "We are aware of the ravens," she said, then asked everyone to stop asking about the buttons. Chapter 9 of the Adventurers' Guild, meanwhile, offered to sell the Constabulary a map to the nest for forty gold pieces. The map is allegedly accurate.

A reward of 25 gold pieces has been posted for any button returned in good condition. The Constabulary is paying in string, which it says goes in the trousers. Residents who spot a raven wearing a Constabulary badge are asked to keep calm and to call the scanner, not the bird.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Button Thieves
hook.text: A swarm of ravens has stripped every brass button, buckle and clasp from the town constabulary's uniforms, and the captain will pay anything to get them back before the baron's inspection. The nest holds more than buttons, including something stolen from a noble's strongbox.

npc.name: Orla Pennick
npc.want: To recover the Constabulary's buttons before the inspection and avoid being the sergeant who lost her trousers.
npc.secret: She sold the Constabulary's spare buttons to a tailor last month and hoped the ravens would cover the shortage.

location.name: The Chimney Nest
location.text: A soot-black chimney on the roof of an abandoned dye works where the ravens keep their hoard. The inside walls are braided with buttons, coins, and one very lost wedding ring.

campaign.rumor: They say the ravens are not thieves at all but a debt collector's spies, and the buttons are just the interest.

articles.title: Gelatinous Cube Replaces 40 Dishwashers at Tavern Chain
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Tankard & Crumb Taverns laid off 40 dishwashers and installed one gelatinous cube in the scullery. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a bold pivot.
articles.content:
Tankard & Crumb Taverns announced Monday that it has laid off 40 dishwashers across its six Hollowpeck locations and replaced them with a single gelatinous cube. The cube is housed in the central scullery and reportedly cleans 900 plates an hour. I call this rightsizing the adventuring party, and frankly, it is the most elegant cost line I have seen all year.

Chief Executive Hob Fennimore unveiled the hire at a breakfast presentation, standing beside the cube in a freshly pressed tabard. "Our new colleague has no sick days, no wage demands, and a remarkable work ethic," he said. "He also absorbs the plates, but we see that as a feature we can scale." The cube has not yet been given a name, only a badge number.

Early results are strong. Tankard & Crumb reports a 62% drop in labor costs and a 100% drop in lingering grease. A few teething issues remain. The cube has dissolved 31 forks, a ladle, and one regional manager's notebook, which the company describes as "an unscheduled data cleanse."

Former dishwasher Pip Larkwater, 29, was less enthusiastic. "I washed those plates for six years," he said, outside the scullery door. "The cube eats the plates." The Servers' Benevolent Lodge has called for a picket. I call that classic union energy: refusing to see that an ooze is simply a more motivated team member.

When I met Guildmaster Dagmar Coldpenny at a gala years ago, she told me, "Sterling, the best employee is the one who cannot read a contract." I think about that every morning during my sword routine. The cube cannot read. The cube also cannot be sued, though a stable boy tried on its behalf.

Fennimore says a second cube is planned for the pantry, subject to a successful pilot and a very large net. Shares of Tankard & Crumb rose 4% on the news. Diners were less moved, mostly because they were still looking for their spoons.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

- Automation is just a coworker with fewer questions.
- Always keep your notebook out of the scullery.
- A layoff is a pivot if you say it with a smile.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Cube in the Scullery
hook.text: A tavern's new gelatinous cube has swallowed something valuable that a guest left behind. The owner will pay the party to retrieve it without killing the cube, which she is afraid is now on payroll.

npc.name: Greta Mossbottom
npc.want: To recover a guest's lost heirloom before the guest returns.
npc.secret: She has been feeding the cube her competitors' menus.

location.name: The Gleaming Tankard
location.text: A tavern whose plates have never been cleaner. The scullery door is always slightly ajar and faintly warm.

campaign.rumor: They say the cube has been seen reading the wage ledger and does not like what it finds.

articles.title: Potion of Healing Labels Must List Side Effects, Guild Rules
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: The Marrowfield Apothecaries' Guild now requires every potion of healing to list dosage and side effects. The label is bigger than the vial.
articles.content:
Friends, the Marrowfield Apothecaries' Guild voted 31 to 4 on Monday to make every potion of healing carry a label listing its dose, its side effects, and what not to drink it with. A fair idea, I say. The trouble is that the first labels run to fourteen inches and the vials are three.

Guildmaster Tamsin Applewick held up a sample at the vote. It wound around the vial six times and then trailed to the floor like a bride's veil. "We have been very thorough," she said. "The warnings include itchy ears, brief singing, and an urge to hug a goat."

The old herbals have always said a medicine should come with plain advice: take it with food, take it after rest, and do not take it at all if you are cross with your mother. And here, for once, is an actual study. A small trial at the Marrowfield infirmary found patients read a short label twice as often as a long one, and a long one hardly at all. I am sorry to say that our healers ran the numbers and found that nobody finishes a fourteen-inch label.

Apothecary Dunmore Greywether, who stocks the biggest shelf in the market, says the new labels have slowed his work. "I have to hire a boy just to unroll them," he told me. "Yesterday a customer sneezed and the label wound itself around his leg."

I did ask the Guild whether a short label might do the job. A clerk told me the Guild is studying the question, and has produced a report on it that is fourteen inches long. I did not read it, friends, and I suspect the report knew.

So here is what I suggest while the Guild finds its scissors. Ask your apothecary the three plain questions: what is it for, how much, and what happens if I take too much? If they cannot answer in one breath, ask for a different apothecary. And never mix a potion with ale, no matter what your cousin says.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there is an app that reads labels aloud. Go outside, Nyx, and read the label on a tree.

Tonight I recommend a plain chicken-and-rice soup, which has a label of exactly one line: chicken, rice, water.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Fourteen-Inch Warning
hook.text: A potion of healing sold in town carries a label that says it causes 'brief singing.' Someone has swapped a batch with a cursed lookalike, and the apothecary needs the party to trace it before the next vial is poured.

npc.name: Dunmore Greywether
npc.want: To sell his stock before the new labels ruin his week.
npc.secret: He wrote the 'urge to hug a goat' warning himself, after a very odd Tuesday.

location.name: Greywether's Long Shelf
location.text: A narrow apothecary stall with a wall of potions, each wrapped in a paper label that touches the floor. Nobody has ever found the end of the longest one.

campaign.rumor: They say the Guild plans to print the labels on bedsheets next, so nobody can claim they didn't see it.

articles.title: Rust Monster Eats 9,000 gp of Iron Pennies at Mint
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: A rust monster ate 9,000 gp of iron pennies at the Brindlemoor mint on Tuesday, and small change is already scarce. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
articles.content:
A rust monster wandered into the Brindlemoor mint on Tuesday and ate roughly 9,000 gp worth of iron pennies, leaving the town with a shortage of small change. Mint officials say the creature came in through the delivery door behind a cart of ingots and was not noticed until the ingots were gone, followed by the cart's axles.

The sum is 30,000 loaves on the current Loaf Index. (I have checked this four times, and a fifth time while eating toast, which felt disrespectful.) That is a great deal of bread to lose to one animal that, by every account, looked pleased with itself afterward.

The Master of the Mint, Hobart Quillfeather, told reporters the stock was meant for the autumn change run, when taverns and bakeries need pennies for the harvest crowds. "We had every penny counted," he said. "Then it was a different number." Quillfeather confirmed that gold and silver were untouched, as the rust monster has no interest in them, and that the mint's remaining copper is now being guarded by a retired watchman with a wooden spoon.

The economics underneath are simpler than they look. Small coins circulate fast. When the supply drops, shops round prices up to the next silver piece because nobody can make change, and a bread that cost seven pennies starts costing ten. Baker Edda Longbottom said she raised her loaf by a penny out of necessity, "and then another one out of principle." By Wednesday, three stalls on Market Row were refusing change altogether and writing "keep the rest, please" on their signs.

Quillfeather says the mint will restamp pennies from copper by the end of next week, using a mending casting to repair what the rust monster only half chewed. The apprentice assigned to the task asked that the creature be removed from the building first, a request the mint called reasonable.

Sterling Vanmoor called the incident "a healthy reset for the penny sector." I would like Mr. Vanmoor to try buying one apple with a silver piece and see how much of the apple he gets back. Meanwhile, the creature has been moved to a stable outside town, where it is eating the gate.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, notes that her boot is leather and therefore of no interest to the monster. She has asked me not to say where it is. What this means for your pantry: carry exact change, and buy your bread before the baker does the arithmetic.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Penny Shortage
hook.text: A rust monster ate the town's iron change and the mint needs it lured out of the stable before it eats the gate and the stable. The mayor will pay well, and merchants are quietly hoarding what coins remain.

npc.name: Hobart Quillfeather
npc.want: To restock the town's small change before the harvest market opens.
npc.secret: He sold part of the iron stock early and blamed the rust monster to cover the gap.

location.name: The Brindlemoor Mint
location.text: A squat stone building with a single delivery door and a floor covered in orange dust. The door's iron hinges have been eaten away and replaced with rope.

campaign.rumor: They say the rust monster only eats iron pennies because it was raised on a smith's apron, and that it'll come back for the ones in your purse.

articles.title: Pit Trap Pay Strike: Undermaw Porters Walk Off the Job
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Sixty-one hireling porters stopped walking point in the Undermaw Tuesday. They want hazard pay for finding every pit trap with their feet.
articles.content:
They put down the poles. Sixty-one hireling porters walked off the job Tuesday at the mouth of the Undermaw, demanding hazard pay for every pit trap they find the hard way. Chapter 9 pays them four silver a day to walk in front of adventuring parties. The porters say that works out to about one silver per fall.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick called the walkout 'a soft pause in our point-position pipeline.' That means nobody wants to go first. He added that Chapter 9 remains 'on track' and that no party has been left without a floor.

The floor is the problem. 'Level Three has forty-two pit traps on the official map,' said Dunmar Quillfoot, a ten-foot-pole bearer for eleven years. 'I've found thirty-nine of them. The map is wrong about the other three, and so is my left knee.' Quillfoot held up a pole worn to a stub. Chapter 9 issues one per season. It deducts the cost of the replacement from his wages.

Hazard pay is the whole demand. The porters also want a proper lunch break, which at present is whenever the party stops screaming, and a rope at the top of every pit they fall into. 'Just a rope,' said Odalie Burrowgate, a lantern carrier. 'Not a good rope. A rope that's there.'

Chapter 9 says it offered a package. The package, read aloud at the picket line by Quillfoot, includes a free hat, a 'resilience workshop,' and an annual Fall Appreciation Day. Fall Appreciation Day is held at the bottom of the pit on Level Two. Nobody laughed. Burrowgate said she had been to the workshop and it was in the pit.

Parties are already feeling it. The Fourth Attempt, licensed to delve Wednesday, sent its own wizard in front with a feather fall spell and a very worried face. 'He's a specialist,' said a spokesman for the party. 'We value his contributions.' The wizard was heard to say that he had not been asked.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said the town is 'aware of the pits' and urged both sides to talk. She also asked adventurers to stop sending their cousins down as replacements. Eight cousins have fallen so far. Six of them are fine and two have joined the union.

Meanwhile Chapter 9 posted a notice on its door seeking 'enthusiastic point-position volunteers, no experience needed, experience not expected.' That is the guild's way of hiring a person to fall down a hole for free. Not one porter has crossed the line, and Quillfoot says the pits will keep.

Bring snacks to the picket if you can. They're out there in the mud, and nobody's falling.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Picket at the Pit
hook.text: Hireling porters have walked off the job at the mouth of a local dungeon, and the guild wants the party to lead its next delve. Settle the strike, scab at your peril, or find out why the guild's trap map is wrong about the other three pits.

npc.name: Dunmar Quillfoot
npc.want: A rope at the top of every pit and four more silver a day.
npc.secret: He drew the corrected trap map himself and sold it to a rival guild last winter.

location.name: The Muddy Picket Line
location.text: A churned field at the dungeon mouth where striking porters keep a smoking brazier and a chalk tally of falls. Someone has hung a tiny hat on every pole stuck in the ground.

campaign.rumor: They say the guild's three missing pits are really one pit that moves at night.

articles.title: Bridge Troll Raises Toll to 3 Copper, Baronies Parley
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: A bridge troll raised the toll on Quillmarch Bridge from two copper to three, and two baronies sent envoys. Tension holds at nine siege-days.
articles.content:
A bridge troll named Gorvash Pennyfist raised the toll on Quillmarch Bridge from two copper pieces to three on Fourthday. The barony of Ashenfold and the barony of Brackwater, who share the only crossing for forty miles, sent envoys to a parley by sundown.

The parley was held on the bridge itself, because the troll would not leave it. Gorvash sat on the east rail. Ashenfold's envoy stood at the west end. Brackwater's envoy stood at the east end, which put him next to the troll and visibly regretting it. The handshake between the two envoys lasted two seconds. Firm. No hidden dagger detected. One envoy did hide a pie, which was declared a field ration and allowed.

Gorvash read a statement. "Costs are up," he said. "Goats are up. Goats are up forty percent. I do not set the goats." Asked whether the third copper piece was a negotiating position, the troll said it was a copper piece. He then asked the envoys to move along, because they were blocking the queue.

The queue stretched back to a hamlet called Lower Dunmoor. Wagoners, a travelling cheesemonger, and a family of six with one very tired donkey waited in the rain while the envoys argued over the word "adjustment." Ashenfold calls the hike a tax. Brackwater calls it a fee. The troll calls it "a toll, like always," and has not moved from that position since he took the bridge nine winters ago.

Ashenfold's envoy, Dame Hesper Orlowe, demanded a return to two copper pieces and an independent audit of the goats. Brackwater's envoy, Sir Tobin Garrick, proposed that both baronies pay the extra copper piece out of a shared fund, which Ashenfold rejected because it had spent the fund on a fence. Brackwater then offered to build a second bridge. Gorvash said he would be glad to take the toll on that one too.

I have covered sieges that moved faster. I have covered a siege where the defenders ate the siege engines. Here nobody has a catapult, nobody has an army, and everybody has a very strong opinion about three coppers. The honest enemy on this bridge is the troll, and he is the only one who has told the truth all week. I respect it. I do not like it.

The ordinary traveller is the casualty, as ever. A shepherd named Edda told this paper she now walks the long way round, which adds two days and one copper piece's worth of blisters. Nobody in either barony has asked her what she thinks. The envoys did, however, issue a joint press release, which this correspondent has fed to the donkey.

The parley resumes at dawn. The troll will be on the rail. The toll stays at three until further notice. Tension holds at nine siege-days, and the goats remain unaudited.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Third Copper Piece
hook.text: A bridge troll has raised his toll and two feuding lords are blaming each other, leaving a river crossing choked with stranded merchants. A guild of wagoners will pay the party to find out why the troll really needs the money before the lords come to blows.

npc.name: Gorvash Pennyfist
npc.want: To keep his bridge and be treated as a business rather than a monster.
npc.secret: He is secretly paying off a debt to a hag who holds the deed to the riverbank.

location.name: Quillmarch Bridge
location.text: A moss-slick stone bridge with a toll booth built into the east rail. A tally of every crossing is chalked on the underside of the arch, going back nine winters, and the numbers do not match the troll's ledger.

campaign.rumor: They say the troll has not raised the toll at all; the envoys have been skimming the extra copper piece for a year.

articles.title: Young Red Dragon Hoard Permit Approved, With Cheese Conditions
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: The Cellars Board approved a young red dragon's hoard extension under Tanner's Row, 4 votes to 1, on condition that the cheese is shared fairly.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR CELLARS BOARD HEARING ROOM, GROUND LEVEL (I checked) — The Cellars Board voted 4 to 1 last night to let Skorvath, the young red dragon, extend its hoard under three Tanner's Row cellars. The permit comes with eleven conditions. Seven concern cheese.

Skorvath's hoard of 11,400 gold pieces already lies beneath the old tannery. The extension adds roughly 3,000 square feet of floor and, the dragon's filing notes, 'no new fires.' It attended in person, folded into the back of the room, and stated for the record that the two earlier fires were 'a matter of record and a matter of regret.' Board Chair Tolly Wend gaveled it in. The gavel survived.

The vote turned on the cheese survey, which found the hoard's heat ripens cheddar in hours. Inspector Corwin Tallowby read the numbers aloud: a wheel that takes eleven months in a normal cellar takes under four hours at the edge of the pile. 'I have classified this as favorable,' Tallowby said. 'I have also classified my own surprise. It is on a separate form.'

The conditions, as filed: Skorvath may not sit on any wheel not its own. Cheese ripened in the hoard must be sold at posted prices, with a third of each batch set aside for the Board's tasting table. The dragon must keep a ten-foot pole's width between the pile and any cellar wall, and I have counted one pole lost to this beat already today. Cellar doors get two keys, one held by the keeper and one by the dragon, so that neither can claim surprise.

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, whose cellar is one of the three, did not oppose the permit. 'It pays rent in cheese,' she said. 'The cube paid in nothing.' She has agreed to a trial: forty wheels, one night, results tomorrow. Her cellar floor was dry-swept for the occasion.

The lone no vote came from Board member Hester Quillfoot, who owns a competing aging cave outside town and was asked to recuse herself. She declined, citing 'a deep personal interest in not being the slow option.' The Board noted the objection and moved on.

Reeve Fennick was seen leaving the hearing with a wedge of cheddar and no comment. When asked, the party's bard, who asked to be named, said he had 'a feeling about the cheese,' then ate it. Hit points at the hearing: Board, 5 of 5; dragon, full; Tallowby, full, except for his composure.

The extension begins at the next new moon. I rolled poorly on last week's cellar prediction, which said the permit would be tabled again, so take this one with a wedge of salt.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: Rent Paid in Cheese
hook.text: A young red dragon has won a permit to extend its hoard under a row of taverns, and its heat ripens cheese in hours. A rival cave owner wants the permit revoked and will pay the party to catch the dragon breaking one of its eleven conditions.

npc.name: Hester Quillfoot
npc.want: To see the dragon's permit revoked before her cave loses its customers.
npc.secret: She has already paid a kobold to scratch a hole in a cellar wall so the pile looks too close.

location.name: The Tanner's Row Cellars
location.text: Three connected tavern cellars sharing a wall with a dragon's hoard. Everything in them is a little warm, and the cheese is always ready.

campaign.rumor: They say the dragon's cheddar is so good that the Board's tasting table has started voting in a block.

articles.title: Autocorrect Wand Turns Fireball Into 'Fire Ball Pit'
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Brightkettle's new Smartcast wand has built-in autocorrect for incantations. Nyx tried a fireball and got a ball pit. Four eyes, singed.
articles.content:
Okay. OKAY. Brightkettle Wandworks launched the Smartcast wand on Tuesday, the first wand with autocorrect for incantations, and I was first in line at the Brindlemoor shop, which opened at nine and ran out of stock at nine-oh-one. The pitch is simple: mispronounce a word and the wand quietly fixes it before the magic goes off. I tested it on a fireball.

The runic latency is wonderful! I said "fireball" at a training dummy, the wand paused for a delicate half second, and the dummy was buried in several hundred bright foam spheres. A clerk at the shop later explained that the wand "learned" from the realm's most common casting phrases, and the word the realm says most near children is, apparently, "ball pit." Nobody was hurt. The dummy is thriving.

Other users have fared worse. Maribel Thornwhistle, a hedge-wizard from the east market, told me her wand changed "light" to "lightning" during a quiet supper. Her stew survived. The ceiling did not. A guard captain on night shift reports his wand rewrote "hold person" into "hold perception," and he has been unable to notice anything since Tuesday, which he says is the same as a normal shift.

Brightkettle's helpful assistant, a tiny spirit who lives in the grip and calls itself Quill, offers suggestions as you cast. "Did you mean: sleep?" it asks, mid-fireball. You can't dismiss it. Quill also wants a Premium tier at 6 gp a month to "stop suggesting." It is a subscription fee for silence, the worst category of fee, and I paid it twice because I lost the receipt.

The wand has an option called Predictive Casting, which finishes your incantation for you. It finished mine with a toast to the health of a distant cousin, at a funeral, aloud. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, now speaks only in ad copy and said, "Smartcast. Say less, mean more." This is both a slogan and a threat. Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to just speak clearly and touch grass. Brother Tumbleberry has never watched a wand finish his sentences in public, and I would sell my entire rune-chip collection to watch him try.

Brightkettle says a patch will ship "as soon as the wand is ready." Support suggests turning the wand off and on again, which in a wand means a short ritual, a candle, and a promise not to tell the wand about its mother.

Verdict: four out of five beholder eyes. The wand understands me better than I understand myself. Unfortunately, it keeps being wrong about it.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 1. Ball pits conjured: 1. Subscription fees paid by mistake: 2. Eyebrows: pending.

hook.title: The Wand That Finished Sentences
hook.text: A shipment of autocorrecting wands has reached the town, and every casting now comes out slightly wrong, from foam-filled halls to a guard who cannot perceive anything. The town wizard will pay the party to trace the wand's spirit to its source before the festival.

npc.name: Maribel Thornwhistle
npc.want: To get a refund and a new roof before the festival.
npc.secret: She has been quietly keeping the wand's spirit fed so it won't be recalled, because it is the only thing that listens to her.

location.name: The Smartcast Counter
location.text: A bright, cluttered wand shop with a queue of apologetic customers. Every wand on the shelf whispers a suggested word when you walk past.

campaign.rumor: They say the wand's spirit has been quietly rewriting the town's marriage vows, and nobody has noticed because they all sound lovely.

articles.title: Doppelganger Held Two Council Seats; Quorum Void
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A doppelganger sat as two members of Brindlemoor's Burgess Council for a year, so every quorum since is void. The Chamber took a recess to discuss it.
articles.content:
The Burgess Council of Brindlemoor learned on Tuesday that a doppelganger has occupied two of its nine seats for roughly a year, which means no quorum call since last autumn was valid. The discovery came when the lady from the Tanner's Ward and the gentleman from the Candle Quarter were seen eating lunch together, in the same coat, from the same plate.

The Council requires seven members present to conduct business. By the clerk's reckoning, seven were present at every sitting, but one of the seven was always two of them. The true count was therefore six, and six is not a quorum under Standing Order 4. I checked. It is on page nine.

The doppelganger, who gave its name to the clerk as Burgess Orrin Tallowby and then, after a pause, as Burgess Wenna Tallowby, declined to speak to the gallery. Through counsel it said it had attended every sitting, read every bill, and voted consistently, which it noted put it ahead of the other seven.

The gentleman from the Cooper's Ward moved that the matter be referred to committee. The lady from the Weir Street Ward objected that the committee also contained the doppelganger. A recess was called. It lasted three hours, during which the Council could not formally agree that it was in recess.

The consequences are considerable. Every ordinance passed in twelve months is now of doubtful standing, including the owlbear leash ordinance, which passed 5-4 last week. The doppelganger voted for it twice. Without those votes it fails 3-4, though the owlbear in the gallery has said it considers the ordinance binding on everyone else regardless.

The clerk, Hobb Pennywhistle, produced the attendance book and showed that the doppelganger signed both names in different hands, one of them left-handed. "I assumed they were twins," he said. "Burgess Tallowby had mentioned a twin. Burgess Tallowby had mentioned a lot of things." Asked why he never raised it, Pennywhistle said nobody had asked him to count the people, only the signatures.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the doppelganger had in fact been the Council's most reliable member. It never missed a vote, never spoke past its allotted time, and was the only member to read the budget. "It was two of the best Burgesses we had," the courtier said. "We have now lost both."

The Council meets again Friday to decide whether Friday counts. By my tally this brings the session's Promises Made to nine, and Promises Kept to the one about holding lunch in public, which was kept more thoroughly than anyone intended. Three members have already announced they will contest the seat of the doppelganger, and one of them is the doppelganger.

The motion to adjourn carried 4-0. Nobody could say who had counted.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Burgess Who Was Two
hook.text: A town council's every decree is thrown into doubt after a doppelganger is found holding two seats. The mayor's office hires the party to find out who else on the council is not who they sign as, before the next vote on the grain tax.

npc.name: Hobb Pennywhistle
npc.want: To prove the attendance book was never his fault before the town audits it.
npc.secret: He noticed the double signatures months ago and kept quiet because the doppelganger filed the only correct minutes.

location.name: The Council Hall Annex
location.text: A cramped side room where the council's attendance books are stored. Every chair has two nameplates, and one of them is always slightly warm.

campaign.rumor: They say the doppelganger was not the only one, and that the lady from the Weir Street Ward has been very quiet since Tuesday.

articles.title: Mimic Posing as Tavern Door Swallows 31 Hats on Fish Street
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A mimic disguised as a tavern door on Fish Street ate 31 hats in three weeks before the Constabulary noticed. Skritch allegedly got his tail stuck.
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell after midnight, the Constabulary was allegedly called to the Rusty Ladle on Fish Street, where a mimic had spent three weeks pretending to be the front door. By the Constabulary's count it ate 31 hats, one eyepatch, and a bard's second-best lute. Nobody noticed because the door, allegedly, always opened.

'I pushed on it every night,' said Gorbin Tuck, a cooper who was eating a pickled egg at the time. 'It felt sticky. I figured the damp.' Tuck lost a wool cap in the second week and blamed a draft.

The trouble started when regulars began going home bareheaded and, in several cases, without their pride. Barmaid Odalie Fenn says she noticed the hat pile was shrinking from the wrong end. 'Customers come in wearing hats. Customers leave not wearing hats. That's not a draft, that's a pattern,' she said, and then served me a very small beer. It was a nice mug, though. Copper rim.

Constabulary Sergeant Brindle Pamm says the mimic was found when a patron tried to leave through the door and the door tried to leave through the patron. 'It had a knocker and everything,' Pamm said. 'Hinges, too. Painted-on hinges. Very convincing hinges.' The patron, a halfling named Dob, was allegedly pulled free by his ankles and is expected to recover his dignity by spring.

I went to see it myself. Allegedly I did not touch the door. Reader, I touched the door. My left foot is still a little sticky and the mimic has, allegedly, my second-best boot. Ooh, also there was a very nice brass knocker lying right there, which I am told is the mimic's actual knocker. I have been told not to take it. Anyway.

The Rusty Ladle's owner, Hesk Varnow, says he installed the door in a hurry last month after a gelatinous mishap and never asked where it came from. 'It was cheap, and it matched the frame,' Varnow said. 'A good door should match the frame.' He has since moved the tavern entrance to a window.

The Constabulary has the mimic in a locked cellar on Tanner's Row, where it is allegedly pretending to be a crate. Wizards from the Tower District have offered to buy it, which tells you everything about the Tower District. The hats, the Constabulary says, will be returned in order of how digested they are.

Pigeons, I note, were seen on the roof the whole time and said nothing. Allegedly in on it.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Door That Ate Hats
hook.text: Patrons of the Silver Pail keep leaving without their hats, and the owner begs the party to find out why before his regulars switch taverns. The culprit is a mimic that has been feeding on caps for weeks and is getting bolder.

npc.name: Odalie Fenn
npc.want: To keep the regulars coming back and get the hats returned.
npc.secret: She sold three of the missing hats to a hatmaker before she realized the door was eating them.

location.name: The Silver Pail
location.text: A cramped tavern with a very sturdy front door that is always slightly warm. The cellar smells like glue.

campaign.rumor: They say the new door at the Pail was hauled out of a dungeon by a drunk adventurer who owed the owner money.

articles.title: Bag of Holding Recall: 3,000 Packs Share One Pocket
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Pettibone & Vail Outfitters recalls 3,000 bags of holding that open into one shared space. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a sharing economy.
articles.content:
Pettibone & Vail Outfitters of Brindlemoor announced Tuesday a recall of 3,000 bags of holding from its Trailmaster line, after customers discovered that every bag in the batch opens into the same extradimensional space. Reeve Maudrey Fennick confirmed that her office has received 412 complaints, most of them from adventurers who reached in for a rope and came out with a stranger's wedding ring, a live goat, or in one case a stranger's grandmother's ashes, which were returned with apologies.

Some people see a defective product. I see the most exciting pooled-asset story of the year. Pettibone & Vail didn't fail, friends. They discovered the sharing economy, and they did it at scale, with 3,000 distribution nodes. Every adventurer in the Trailmaster network now has access to the combined inventory of every other adventurer. Try getting that from a mere backpack.

The company's spokesman, a cheerful gnome named Dorlic Pettibone-Vail (no relation, he says, to either founder), called the recall "a proactive realignment of ownership expectations." Refunds are available in coin, or in whatever the customer's bag was holding, whichever the customer can find.

The trouble was first noticed at the Sleeping Mule, where Keeper Bess Harrowgate watched four separate parties argue over one shared supply of 900 torches, all of which appeared to be in all of their bags at once. By nightfall the pocket held, per one tally, 61 bedrolls, a dozen ladders, an unlicensed owlbear cub, and a ledger from Shieldwall Mutual denying coverage for exactly this. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said Chapter 9 considers the matter "on track" and has begun charging a retrieval fee.

Naturally the regulators are circling. Reeve Fennick said only, "We are aware of the pocket." I'd rather not comment on a body that thinks a 400-complaint rounding error needs a permit. Meanwhile, an unnamed shop steward at the Outfitters' Brindlemoor warehouse, one of those union types, has demanded hazard pay for staff who reach in to sort the returns. Fourteen of them have been rightsized to the other side of the bag, where, I'm told, the networking is excellent.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove once, at a spring gala in a hot-air balloon. He told me, "Sterling, never own what you can lease from a stranger's pocket." I have thought about it every morning since, during my sword routine.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A shared bag of holding is a community. Label your goat.
  • Disruption always starts with 412 complaints.
  • If it is in the pocket, it is liquid.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Pocket Everyone Shares
hook.text: A merchant's whole caravan inventory has vanished into a bag of holding that opens into a shared pocket, and a rival's party is selling it back. The party must find the other bags before the pocket's contents are sold off, and before something living in it gets hungry.

npc.name: Dorlic Fenwhistle
npc.want: To clear the recall backlog before his employer notices his own bag is part of it.
npc.secret: He has been quietly pulling valuables from the shared pocket for a week.

location.name: The Retrieval Counter
location.text: A refund window in a warehouse where claimants line up to reach into one bag and describe what they lost. The floor is covered in goats.

campaign.rumor: They say the pocket has grown a back room, and someone is already renting it out.

articles.title: 3 Owlbear Cubs Found in Undermaw; Chapter 9 Says 'Visitors'
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: Three owlbear cubs were found shivering on Level Four of the Undermaw. Chapter 9 calls them visitors. Brother Wendell calls for milk, blankets and naps.
articles.content:
Friends, three owlbear cubs were found curled in a collapsed supply cart on Level Four of the Undermaw on Monday, hungry, cold and very loud. A scouting party of the Fourth Attempt carried them up to Brindlemoor in a bread basket, and the whole town has been tiptoeing around the Tanner's Row stables ever since.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 told reporters the cubs are not a monster incident. "They are visitors from a lower level, and the arrival is on track," he said, handing out a form with a box for each cub's claws. Reeve Fennick, asked for comment, said, "We are aware of the cubs," and then went to sit down in the stables for twenty minutes without speaking.

Now the useful part. The old herbals say a motherless young thing wants warmth, quiet, and small meals often. The new studies on young animals agree: keep them warm, feed them on a schedule, and handle them as little as you can manage, because stress slows growth. I stood in that stable for an hour and can report that the cubs have grown in two days from the size of a loaf to the size of a very rude loaf. Each now eats a pail of goat milk at dawn, noon and dusk, then falls asleep mid-hoot like a proper cleric after a long vigil.

Not everyone is calm. A local pawnbroker offered forty gold for a cub, and a bard has already written a ballad called "Hoot of My Heart," which has eleven verses and no rhyme for owlbear. Let the record show I looked at the pawnbroker the way my grandmother looked at burnt toast, and he left. The young ones are not loot, friends, and they are not content. They are babies, and babies need rest.

A word on the milk. Goat milk is fine, but cow milk gives them the runs, and a cub with the runs is a thing no stable should have to endure. Please do not bring the cubs honey cakes, however they beg. The Brindlemoor Sage Circle will examine them on Thursday and decide where a wild creature belongs, and I have written to ask that the answer be a meadow rather than a menagerie.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil asked whether there is a gadget that translates owlbear. There is, Nyx, it is called sitting quietly and listening. Go outside, Nyx. Tonight I recommend a bowl of creamy potato-and-chive soup, which the cubs refuse and I do not.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: Hoot of the Orphaned
hook.text: Three owlbear cubs have been carried out of a dungeon, and their mother, enraged and searching, is following the trail toward the party's town. A druid wants the cubs returned to the wild before she arrives; a fence wants them sold.

npc.name: Tilda Weatherbury
npc.want: To raise the cubs safely and release them in a quiet meadow.
npc.secret: She has already been paid by a collector who will take one cub tonight.

location.name: The Tanner's Row Stables
location.text: A drafty stable turned nursery, its stalls lined with blankets and warning signs. Every hour a different neighbor sneaks in to peek at the cubs.

campaign.rumor: I heard the mother owlbear has already tunneled up past Level Two, and she is not asking nicely.

articles.title: Red Dragon's 2.4M gp Hoard Is Mostly Painted Copper
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Waterdeep lenders who took a red dragon's hoard as collateral for a 1.2M gp loan found 80% of it was painted copper. Barnaby did the sums. Four times.
articles.content:
A red dragon's hoard, pledged as collateral for a 1.2 million gp loan, was appraised at 2.4 million gp and is actually worth about 480,000 gp, Waterdeep lenders said on Wednesday. Roughly four coins in five were copper pieces under gold paint. The dragon, Cindrakel, has not repaid a coin. On the Loaf Index, the missing 1.92 million gp is about 6.4 million loaves. (I have checked this four times, and then once with a candle.)

Here is how the lending works. A lender hands out money against something valuable and keeps the right to take that something if the borrower stops paying. This only works if the collateral is what it claims to be. The Gilded Ledger Syndicate valued the hoard by weighing it, and a dragon lying on a heap makes a heap seem heavy. Copper is lighter than gold, but there was a great deal of it, and nobody thought to scrape one.

Syndicate partner Wendeline Ashcombe said the paint job was "remarkably even" and that the dragon "was very warm and reassuring during the appraisal." She would not say who held the brush. Cindrakel's own counsel says the hoard was always described as "gold-colored," which is a phrase that now appears, underlined, in 3,200 pages of loan paperwork.

The Syndicate then did what lenders do and tried to sell the hoard on to other lenders in a bundle. Four of them had already bought slices. One slice reached a widows' pension fund, which put aside 90,000 gp against it and now owns a pile of painted copper the size of a cart. A clerk there told me, "We were told it was dragon-backed." It was, in the sense that a dragon was on top of it.

The pantry feels this next. Dragon-hoard loans are priced as safe, because a dragon is hard to sue. If a hoard can be mostly paint, the lenders must reprice every other one, and the cost of borrowing against a hoard stashed in a bag of holding rises. Flour sellers who borrow to stock up, as that miller did, will pay more. Bread follows.

My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot, and has been asked by three neighbors this morning whether the boot is gold or merely gold-colored. It is leather. She said so to each of them, calmly, and then looked at me. I did not laugh.

The Syndicate says it will seize whatever is left. Cindrakel has said she will consider it, after a nap. A red dragon's nap can last a decade, and interest accrues daily. The Syndicate's lawyers have already asked whether paint counts as a lien.

What this means for your pantry: buy flour now, and scrape one coin before you trust a pile.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: Gold-Colored
hook.text: A lending house has been burned by a hoard of painted copper and offers the party 5,000 gp to find who painted it before the dragon wakes and wants her loan forgiven. Someone in town sold a hundred barrels of gold paint last spring.

npc.name: Wendeline Ashcombe
npc.want: To trace the painter and recover something for her investors.
npc.secret: She signed off on the appraisal without scraping one coin because she was told the dragon dislikes being inconvenienced.

location.name: The Painted Hoard Cavern
location.text: A cavern floor of coins that gleam in lamplight and flake in daylight. Gold dust drifts from the ceiling when the dragon sighs.

campaign.rumor: I heard the dragon painted it herself, because she thought it looked more like gold that way.

articles.title: Owlbear Crosswalk: Crossing Guards Demand Hazard Pay
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Six Brindlemoor crossing guards stopped working the Tanner's Row crosswalk Wednesday. An owlbear uses it daily at the school bell, and the pay is 4 silver.
articles.content:
They put down the stop-signs. Six school crossing guards in Brindlemoor refused Wednesday to work the Tanner's Row crosswalk until the town pays hazard pay for an owlbear that crosses it every morning at the school bell.

The town's offer so far is a reflective vest. That means it is the same job with a brighter target.

The owlbear arrived three weeks ago, climbing up from the Undermaw through a drain behind the pawnshop. It crosses at 8:10, in the middle of the schoolchildren, and goes to the dumpling cart. It has not hurt anyone. It has hugged a mule. "The mule was fine," said Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor. "We are aware of the owlbear."

The guards are not asking for the owlbear to be removed. They are asking to be paid for standing next to it. Current pay is 4 silver a morning, with no healing coverage. "I hold a pole with a sign on it," said Odalie Brackenthwaite, a crossing guard for eleven years. "The sign says STOP. The owlbear can't read. I've checked. I held it up for a week."

Her colleague Tomm Gristlewick, a guard on the south corner, said the job has changed. "I used to count children. Now I count children and then I count the owlbear's claws. Claws are not in my contract. Neither is the beak."

The town's reply came from the Office of Streets and Lanterns, which called the owlbear "a seasonal traffic pattern." That means it is not their problem. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 was asked whether the Guild would take the owlbear back into the dungeon. He said the situation was "on track" and that the owlbear was "technically a soft launch of Level Seven."

Brakka went down to the crosswalk at 8:10 Wednesday. The guards were on strike, so nobody was in the road, and the owlbear crossed anyway. Eleven children crossed with it. A parent held a hand over the youngest one's eyes and another gave the owlbear a dumpling, which it ate with the dignity of a magistrate. Then it went home. The Guild issued no comment on whether it wanted the dumpling cart.

The sums are simple. The porters struck last week in the pay strike in Undermaw, and these guards want the same word in their contract: hazard. The town budgeted 90 gold for the crosswalk this year, and the Reeve's own horse stable got 400.

The guards will picket the crosswalk daily at 8:00 sharp. They say they will stop for the owlbear, for the children, and for a proper lunch break, in that order. The schoolmaster has asked parents to walk their children to the school gate the long way round, past the tannery, which smells worse than an owlbear and has never hugged anyone.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Crosswalk Strike
hook.text: The crossing guards of a market town have walked out because a hungry owlbear now crosses the school road each morning. The schoolmaster wants it lured away before the picket collapses, and the parents will pay in dumplings.

npc.name: Odalie Brackenthwaite
npc.want: To be paid properly for eleven years of standing in front of danger.
npc.secret: She has been feeding the owlbear dumplings herself so it will keep its route and keep her pay claim alive.

location.name: Tanner's Row Crosswalk
location.text: A broad cobbled crossing between a schoolhouse and a dumpling cart. A worn pair of claw marks runs along the curb like a second set of road lines.

campaign.rumor: They say the owlbear isn't wild at all, that it belonged to a retired adventurer who died owing the pawnshop money.

articles.title: Rust Monster Eats Border Gate; Tourists Cross Free
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: A rust monster ate the iron gate at Greywater Crossing on Fourthday. Two baronies dispute the bill while 3,000 travelers walk through untaxed.
articles.content:
A rust monster ate the iron border gate at Greywater Crossing on Fourthday, all eleven tons of it, and left the frontier open for the first time in 212 years. Two baronies now argue over who owes the rebuild. Tourists, meanwhile, are crossing without paying a copper.

The monster arrived at dawn. Guard Sergeant Helga Brandt of the northern post reports it ate the hinges first, then the bars, then the toll booth's cashbox. "It took the lock last," she said. "Politely, I thought." The beast is now asleep in the customs shed, full and rust-colored, surrounded by the barons' envoys at a respectful distance of forty feet.

The parley opened at noon. Baron Osric Tallowmere of the north demanded the south pay for the gate, since the monster came from southern marshland. Baroness Edda Pike of the south replied that the gate was northern iron, northern property, and a northern snack. Handshake: firm, three seconds, one envoy checked his own ring finger afterward. No hidden dagger detected. Nobody had a dagger. The monster had eaten those too.

Siege-days stand at four. That is low for a border dispute and high for a gate.

Tourism is the winner, as it always is when leaders stop talking. An estimated 3,000 travelers crossed the open frontier by Sixthday, a crowd that normally takes nine days to clear the tax queue. Innkeeper Marta Wynn of the Crooked Lantern says her rooms are full and her guests are the happiest she has seen. "Nobody has been fined for their luggage," she said. "One man asked if he had been robbed. We said no. He cried."

Both baronies have since filed press statements calling the incident a "moment of regional opportunity." I have read them both. They are the same statement. One changed the baron's name. I hate press releases, and these were not even good ones.
